lessons.title: Hello, Python! Your First Program
lessons.explain: The print() function displays text on the screen. Text wrapped in quotes is called a string. This is the traditional first step in every programming language — and every Python journey.
takeaways: print() sends output to the screen — your program talking back to you.
Text in quotes ("..." or '...') is called a string.
Python runs top to bottom, one line at a time.
lessons.code:
print("Hello, Skillzify!")
print("I am learning Python 🚀")

quiz.q: What does print("Hi") do?
quiz.why: print() sends text to the program's output — usually your screen or console.

quiz.q: In Python, text wrapped in quotes is called a…
quiz.why: Quoted text is a string (str) — one of Python's core data types.

quiz.q: What does this print? print("Py", "thon")
quiz.why: print() separates multiple arguments with a space.

quiz.q: In this code, which line prints first? print("one") then print("two")
quiz.why: Python runs code top to bottom, one line at a time.

quiz.q: What is wrong with print(Hello)?
options: Hello must be in quotes to be a string
quiz.why: Without quotes, Python reads Hello as a variable name, which does not exist.

challenge.hint: With strings, + joins (concatenates) them instead of adding.

lessons.title: Variables & Data Types
lessons.explain: Variables store values under a name. Python figures out the type automatically — int for whole numbers, float for decimals, str for text, and bool for True/False. Think of a variable as a labelled box you can put things in and swap out later.
takeaways: Create a variable with name = value — no type declaration needed.
Core types: int, float, str, bool. Check with type().
Variable names use letters, digits, _ — and can't start with a digit.
lessons.code:
name = "Vikas"
age = 20
height = 5.9
is_student = True

print(name, age, height, is_student)
print(type(age))  # <class 'int'>

quiz.q: What is the type of x = 3.14?
quiz.why: A number with a decimal point is a float (floating-point).

quiz.q: Which is a valid variable name?
quiz.why: Names can't start with a digit, can't contain '-', and can't be Python keywords like class.

quiz.q: What does this print? x = 5, then x = x + 2, then print(x)
quiz.why: x is reassigned: 5 + 2 = 7.

quiz.q: Which assignment fails?
quiz.why: Hyphens are not allowed in names — Python reads it as subtraction.

quiz.q: After a = 10 and b = a, what is b?
quiz.why: b copies a's current value, which is 10.

challenge.prompt: Fill the blank so the program prints 25:
challenge.code:
age = ____
print(age + 5)  # should print 25
challenge.hint: age + 5 = 25, so age must be the integer 20.

lessons.title: Strings & f-strings
lessons.explain: f-strings let you embed variables directly inside text using curly braces — just prefix the string with f. They're the cleanest, fastest way to build messages in modern Python, and you'll use them everywhere.
takeaways: Prefix a string with f to embed {expressions} inside it.
String methods like .upper(), .lower(), .strip() return new strings.
len(s) gives the number of characters in a string.
lessons.code:
name = "Vikas"
score = 95

message = f"{name} scored {score} marks!"
print(message)
print(name.upper())
print(len(name))

quiz.q: What does f"{name}!" do?
quiz.why: The f prefix turns {name} into the variable's value inside the string.

quiz.q: What is len("Python")?
quiz.why: P-y-t-h-o-n = 6 characters.

quiz.q: What does this print? s = "hello", then print(s.upper())
quiz.why: .upper() returns a new all-caps string.

quiz.q: What does this print? x = 5, then print(f"{x + 1}")
quiz.why: f-strings can evaluate any expression inside the braces.

quiz.q: After s = "abc" and s.upper(), what is s?
quiz.why: String methods return new strings; they never change the original.

challenge.code:
s = "abc"
print(s.upper() + str(len(s)))
challenge.hint: s.upper() → "ABC", len(s) → 3, str(3) → "3", then + joins them.

lessons.title: Conditionals: if / elif / else
lessons.explain: Conditionals let your program make decisions. Python checks each condition top to bottom and runs the first block that is True. Indentation (4 spaces) defines which lines belong to each block — get it wrong and Python complains.
takeaways: if / elif / else chain: first True condition wins, the rest are skipped.
Conditions use comparisons: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=
Indentation is syntax in Python — it defines code blocks.

quiz.q: With marks = 82, what prints?
quiz.why: 82 >= 90 is False, 82 >= 75 is True → the elif branch runs.

quiz.q: Which keyword tests another condition after if?
quiz.why: elif is short for 'else if' — Python's own keyword.

quiz.q: What prints? x = 5, if x > 10: print("big"), else: print("small")
quiz.why: 5 > 10 is False, so the else branch runs.

quiz.q: In an if / elif / else chain, how many branches run?
quiz.why: Python runs the first branch whose condition is true, then skips the rest.

quiz.q: What is wrong with: if score = 100: ?
quiz.why: = stores a value; == compares two values.

challenge.hint: These are two separate if statements — both conditions are True, so both run.

lessons.title: Loops: for & while
lessons.explain: Loops repeat work without repeating code. A for loop walks through a sequence — range(n) gives 0 … n-1. A while loop repeats while its condition stays True. The classic beginner bug: a while loop whose condition never becomes False runs forever!
takeaways: for i in range(5) loops with i = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
while repeats while its condition is True — make sure it can end.
break exits a loop immediately; continue skips to the next round.
lessons.code:
print("For loop:")
for i in range(1, 6):
    print(f"  2 x {i} = {2 * i}")

print("While loop:")
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(f"  Countdown: {count}")
    count -= 1
print("Go! 🚀")

quiz.q: What numbers does range(1, 6) produce?
quiz.why: range(start, stop) includes start but stops before stop.

quiz.q: What does break do inside a loop?
quiz.why: break jumps straight out of the loop. (continue skips to the next iteration.)

quiz.q: What does this print? for i in range(3): print(i)
quiz.why: range(3) starts at 0 and stops before 3.

quiz.q: What makes while True: dangerous?
options: It loops forever unless break runs
quiz.why: True never becomes False, so only break can stop it.

quiz.q: What prints? for i in range(5): if i == 2: continue, then print(i)
quiz.why: continue skips the rest of that round, so 2 is never printed.

challenge.code:
total = 0
for i in range(4):
    total += i
print(total)

lessons.title: Lists & Tuples
lessons.explain: Lists let you keep an ordered collection of items you can change — perfect for things like to-do lists or scores. Tuples look similar but are locked after creation, which makes them great for fixed data like coordinates. Knowing when to use each one is a core Python habit.
takeaways: Lists are ordered and changeable — index them from 0, or from -1 for the end.
append() adds to the end; slicing like [1:3] grabs a sub-list.
Tuples are immutable — use them for fixed data you do not want accidentally changed.
lessons.code:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
fruits.append("mango")
print(fruits[0])
print(fruits[1:3])
point = (3, 4)
print(point)

quiz.q: What does fruits.append("mango") do?
options: Adds mango to the end of the list
Replaces the first item with mango
quiz.why: append() always adds the new item at the end of the list.

quiz.q: What happens if you try point[0] = 5 on a tuple?
quiz.why: Tuples are immutable, so item assignment raises a TypeError.

quiz.q: What does this print? fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"], then print(fruits[1:3])
quiz.why: Slicing [1:3] takes indices 1 and 2.

quiz.q: What does this print? a = [1, 2], b = a, b.append(3), print(a)
quiz.why: b refers to the same list object as a, so the change is visible through a.
The tuple holds two items.

challenge.code:
nums = [10, 20, 30]
print(nums[-1])
challenge.hint: Negative indexes count from the end of the list.

lessons.title: Dictionaries & Sets
lessons.explain: Dictionaries store data as key-value pairs, so you can look things up by name instead of by position — like a real dictionary. Sets are unordered collections that automatically drop duplicates, which makes them perfect for membership tests. Together they power everything from counting words to removing repeats.
takeaways: Dictionaries map keys to values; look up with d[key] or the safer d.get(key, default).
Assigning to a new key adds it; assigning to an existing key updates it.
Sets store unique items only — duplicates vanish automatically.

quiz.q: What does student.get("grade", "N/A") return when "grade" is missing?
quiz.why: .get() returns the default you supply instead of raising a KeyError.

quiz.q: Why does {"red", "blue", "red"} end up with only two items?
options: The last item overwrites the first
quiz.why: A set can only hold unique values, so the repeated "red" is dropped.

quiz.q: What does this print? d = {"x": 1}, d["x"] = 9, print(d["x"])
quiz.why: Assigning to an existing key overwrites its value.

quiz.q: "z" in {"a", "b"} is…
quiz.why: in tests membership, and "z" is not in the set.

quiz.q: What does this print? s = {3, 1, 2}, print(len(s))
quiz.why: The set holds three unique items.

challenge.prompt: Fill the blank so the program prints 21:
challenge.hint: Dictionary keys go inside the square brackets.

lessons.title: Conditionals & Logic
lessons.explain: Programs get smart when they can make decisions, and conditionals are how you teach them. if/elif/else lets your code take different paths based on what is true right now. Combined with and, or, and not, you can express surprisingly subtle logic in just a few lines.
takeaways: if/elif/else runs the first branch whose condition is true.
and needs both sides true; or needs just one; not flips a condition.
Comparisons can chain: 1 < x < 10 checks both ends at once.

quiz.q: What prints when score is 85?
quiz.why: 85 is not >= 90, but it is >= 75, so the elif branch runs.

quiz.q: In "if x > 5 and x < 10:", when does the block run?
options: Only when both conditions are true
quiz.why: and requires the left and right conditions to both be true.

quiz.q: What does this print? x = 7, print(1 < x < 10)
quiz.why: Chained comparisons check both ends: 1 < 7 and 7 < 10.

quiz.q: not (5 > 3) is…
quiz.why: 5 > 3 is True, and not flips it to False.

quiz.q: What prints? age = 16, print("teen" if 13 <= age <= 19 else "other")
quiz.why: 16 is between 13 and 19, so the condition is True.

challenge.hint: 30 is greater than 25, so the first branch runs.

lessons.title: Loops: for & while — Practice
lessons.explain: Loops let you repeat work without repeating code — the moment a program needs to do something a hundred times, you need them. for loops walk through collections and ranges, while while loops keep going until a condition changes. break and continue give you fine control over when to stop or skip.
takeaways: for i in range(n) loops n times with i going 0 to n-1.
while repeats until its condition becomes false — make sure it eventually does.
break exits the loop now; continue skips to the next round.
lessons.code:
for i in range(3):
    print(i)
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count = count - 1
print("Go!")

quiz.q: What does range(3) produce?
quiz.why: range(3) starts at 0 and stops before 3.

quiz.q: What does break do inside a loop?
quiz.why: break exits the loop right away; continue is the one that skips ahead.

quiz.q: What does this print? total = 0, for i in range(1, 4): total += i, print(total)
n starts at 3 and a while n > 0 loop does n -= 1 each round. How many rounds run?
quiz.why: n goes 3, 2, 1, then 0 stops the loop — 3 rounds.

quiz.q: What prints? for c in "ab": print(c)
quiz.why: for walks through each character of the string in order.

challenge.code:
total = 0
for n in [1, 2, 3]:
    total = total + n
print(total)
challenge.hint: Add them up step by step: 0+1, then +2, then +3.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.explain: Functions let you package logic into reusable, named blocks — write once, call anywhere. Parameters make them flexible, return values make them useful, and default arguments make them friendly. Good functions are the difference between a script and a program.
takeaways: def names a function; parameters are its inputs, return sends a result back.
Arguments with defaults (name="friend") are optional when calling.
A function without return gives back None.
lessons.code:
def greet(name="friend"):
    return "Hello, " + name

print(greet("Asha"))
print(greet())

quiz.q: What does return do in a function?
options: Sends a value back to the caller
quiz.why: return hands a value back to whoever called the function.

quiz.q: What prints for greet() with no arguments?
quiz.why: The default "friend" is used when no argument is given.

quiz.q: What does this print? def double(n): return n * 2, then print(double(5))
quiz.why: double(5) returns 10, which print displays.

quiz.q: With def add(a, b=0):, which call is valid?
quiz.why: b has a default, so only a is required.

quiz.q: What is wrong with a def line that has no colon at the end?
options: Missing colon after the def line
quiz.why: def lines must end with a colon before the indented body.

challenge.prompt: Fill the blank so the program prints 12:
challenge.hint: The function must send the result back to the caller.

lessons.title: Numbers & Math in Python
lessons.explain: Python does arithmetic the way you expect, plus a few bonus operators: // for floor division, % for the remainder, and ** for powers. Whole numbers are ints, decimals are floats, and mixing them always gives a float.
takeaways: `//` divides and rounds down, `%` gives the remainder — together they split totals, like minutes into hours and minutes.
`**` raises to a power: `2 ** 10` is 1024.
Mixing an int and a float always gives a float: `3 + 0.5` is `3.5`.
lessons.code:
print(7 / 2)
print(7 // 2)
print(7 % 2)
print(2 ** 4)

quiz.q: What does `print(10 % 3)` output?
quiz.why: 10 divided by 3 is 3 with remainder 1, and % gives the remainder.

quiz.q: What is the value of `2 ** 3`?
quiz.why: ** means 'to the power of': 2 * 2 * 2 = 8.

quiz.q: What type is the result of `4 + 1.5`?
quiz.why: Adding an int and a float always produces a float.

challenge.code: print(2 ** 3)
challenge.hint: ** means 'to the power of', not multiplication.

lessons.title: String Methods You Will Use Daily
lessons.explain: Strings come with built-in tools called methods. Just a few — strip(), upper(), replace(), split() and join() — handle most everyday text jobs like cleaning up input or building messages.
takeaways: String methods return a NEW string; the original never changes, so write `s = s.strip()`.
`split()` breaks text into a list; `' '.join(parts)` glues a list back into text.
`strip()` removes whitespace from both ends — perfect for tidying user input.
lessons.code:
name = "  Ada  "
print(name.strip())
print(name.strip().upper())
words = "red,blue,green".split(",")
print(words)

quiz.q: What does `'  hello  '.strip()` return?
quiz.why: strip() removes the whitespace from both ends, leaving 'hello'.

quiz.q: After `s = 'a,b,c'` and `parts = s.split(',')`, what is `parts`?
quiz.why: split(',') cuts the string at each comma into a list of three items.

quiz.q: Does `'Hi'.upper()` change the original string?
options: No — strings are immutable, it returns a new one
Yes, it edits the string in place
Only if you assign it back
quiz.why: Strings can't be changed in place; upper() builds and returns a new string.

challenge.code: print("one two".split())
challenge.hint: split() with no arguments splits on any whitespace.

lessons.title: Slicing & Indexing Strings
lessons.explain: Every character in a string has a position starting at 0. Indexing with s[i] grabs one character, and slicing with s[start:stop] grabs a range — the start is included but the stop is left out.
takeaways: Indexes start at 0; negative indexes count from the end, so `s[-1]` is the last character.
In `s[start:stop]`, start is included but stop is excluded.
`s[::-1]` reverses a string — a trick worth memorizing.
lessons.code:
s = "Python"
print(s[0])
print(s[-1])
print(s[0:4])
print(s[::-1])

quiz.q: If `s = 'Python'`, what is `s[1]`?
quiz.why: Counting starts at 0, so index 1 is the second character, 'y'.

quiz.q: What does `'Python'[1:4]` give?
quiz.why: It takes indexes 1, 2 and 3 ('y', 't', 'h'); index 4 is excluded.

quiz.q: What is the value of `'abc'[-1]`?
quiz.why: Negative indexes count from the end, so -1 is the last character.

challenge.code: print('hello'[1:4])
challenge.hint: Counting starts at 0, and the stop index is left out.

lessons.title: Type Conversion & the input() Function
lessons.explain: input() always returns text, even when the user types a number — so convert it with int() or float() before doing math. The same conversion functions switch between types anywhere: int('7') becomes 7, str(7) becomes '7'.
takeaways: `input()` returns a string — wrap it: `age = int(input('Age: '))`.
`int('7')` gives 7, `str(7)` gives '7', `float('2.5')` gives 2.5.
Converting bad text like `int('abc')` raises a ValueError.
lessons.code:
age_text = "21"
age = int(age_text)
print(age + 4)
print("Next year: " + str(age + 1))

quiz.q: If `n = input()` and the user types 5, what does `n + 1` do?
options: Raises TypeError — can't add int to str
quiz.why: n is the string '5', and adding a string and an int is a TypeError.

quiz.q: What does `int('42') + 8` equal?
quiz.why: int('42') becomes the number 42 first, then 42 + 8 = 50.

quiz.q: What does `str(3.5)` return?
quiz.why: str() converts the float into its text form, '3.5'.

challenge.code: print(int("10") * 2)
challenge.hint: int('10') becomes the number 10 before the multiplication.

lessons.title: Boolean Logic: and, or, not
lessons.explain: and, or and not combine True/False values into decisions. `and` needs both sides true, `or` needs just one, and `not` flips a value — they're the building blocks of every if statement with multiple conditions.
takeaways: `and` is True only when BOTH sides are True; `or` needs just ONE.
`not` flips a value: `not True` is False.
Comparisons return booleans, so `age >= 18 and has_ticket` reads like English.
lessons.code:
age = 20
has_ticket = True
print(age >= 18 and has_ticket)
print(age < 13 or not has_ticket)

quiz.q: What is `True and False`?
quiz.why: and needs both sides True, but one side is False.

quiz.q: What is `True or False`?
quiz.why: or needs only one side True, and the left side is True.

quiz.q: What does `not (5 > 3)` evaluate to?
quiz.why: 5 > 3 is True, and not flips it to False.

challenge.code:
x = 7
print(x > 5 and x < 10)
challenge.hint: Is 7 both greater than 5 AND less than 10?

lessons.title: Nested Loops & Patterns
lessons.explain: A loop inside another loop runs the inner loop fully for every single step of the outer one. That's exactly what you need to draw grids and patterns — think of the outer loop as rows and the inner loop as columns.
takeaways: The inner loop completes ALL its iterations for each ONE iteration of the outer loop.
Use `print(..., end='')` to stay on the same line; a bare `print()` moves down a row.
Outer loop = rows, inner loop = columns is the mental model for patterns.

quiz.q: How many times does print run here? `for i in range(2):` then `for j in range(3): print(j)`
quiz.why: The inner loop runs 3 times for each of the 2 outer iterations: 2 x 3 = 6.

quiz.q: What does `print('a', end='')` followed by `print('b')` output?
options: a then b on separate lines
quiz.why: end='' replaces the newline, so 'b' prints right after 'a'.

quiz.q: In a pattern program, the outer loop usually represents…
quiz.why: Each outer iteration draws one full row; the inner loop draws its columns.

challenge.code:
for i in range(2):
    print(i, end="-")
challenge.hint: end='-' replaces the newline after each print.

lessons.title: break, continue & Loop else
lessons.explain: break exits a loop immediately, continue skips to the next iteration, and a loop's else block runs only if the loop finished without break — perfect for 'search and not found' logic.
takeaways: `break` stops the whole loop; `continue` skips just the current round.
A `for...else` runs its else only when NO break happened.
Use break for 'found it, stop looking' searches.

quiz.q: What does `break` do inside a loop?
quiz.why: break jumps straight out of the loop; nothing after it in the loop runs.

quiz.q: When does a `for...else` block's else run?
options: Only if the loop never hit break
Only if the loop body is empty
quiz.why: The else means 'completed normally' — a break skips it.

quiz.q: What prints? `for i in range(5):` `if i == 2: continue` `print(i, end='')`
quiz.why: continue skips only the iteration where i is 2; the rest print.

challenge.hint: The loop stops the moment i becomes 2.

lessons.title: Function Arguments: Defaults & Keywords
lessons.explain: Parameters can have default values, so callers may skip them — and any argument can be passed by name (keyword), which makes calls readable and frees you from remembering the order.
takeaways: A default like `def greet(name='friend')` makes that argument optional.
Keyword arguments name the parameter: `greet(name='Ada')`.
Once a parameter has a default, every parameter after it needs one too.
lessons.code:
def greet(name, punct="!"):
    print("Hi " + name + punct)
greet("Ada")
greet("Bob", punct="?")
greet(name="Zoe", punct=".")

quiz.q: Given `def f(a, b=5)`, which call is valid?
quiz.why: f(1) sets a=1 and b falls back to 5; the others break argument rules.

quiz.q: What is `greet(name='Ada')` using?
quiz.why: Naming the parameter at the call site is a keyword argument.

quiz.q: Why is `def f(a=1, b):` invalid?
options: A non-default parameter can't follow a default one
quiz.why: Python requires all defaulted parameters to come after the required ones.

challenge.hint: b falls back to its default of 10.

lessons.title: Scope: Local vs Global
lessons.explain: A variable created inside a function is local — it exists only while the function runs. Code outside can't see it, and a local with the same name as a global shadows (hides) it without changing the original.
takeaways: Local variables die when the function returns; they can't be used outside.
Reading a global inside a function is fine; assigning to it creates a NEW local unless you write `global`.
Same name inside and outside? The inner one wins — but only inside.
lessons.code:
x = 10
def show():
    x = 99
    print(x)
show()
print(x)

quiz.q: What prints? `x = 1` then `def f():` `x = 2` then `f()` then `print(x)`
quiz.why: The x inside f() is a separate local; the global x stays 1.

quiz.q: Can code outside a function read a variable created inside it?
options: No — it is local to the function
Only if it holds a number
quiz.why: Local variables exist only during the function's execution.

quiz.q: What does the `global` keyword do?
options: Lets a function assign to a module-level variable
quiz.why: Without it, assignment inside a function creates a local instead.

challenge.code:
n = 5
def change():
    n = 0
change()
print(n)
challenge.hint: The n inside change() is a separate local variable.

lessons.title: Docstrings & Getting Help
lessons.explain: A docstring is a triple-quoted string right under a function's def line that documents what it does. Python's help() shows it, and good docstrings make your future self (and teammates) grateful.
takeaways: A docstring is the FIRST statement in a function, written in triple quotes.
`help(func)` prints the docstring; `func.__doc__` gives it as a string.
One line for what it does, plus the parameters, is enough for small functions.
lessons.code:
def square(n):
    """Return n multiplied by itself."""
    return n * n
print(square.__doc__)

quiz.q: Where does a docstring go?
options: As the first statement inside the function
At the end of the file
quiz.why: Python treats the first string literal in a function body as its documentation.

quiz.q: What does `help(len)` do?
quiz.why: help() displays the docstring and signature of any object.

quiz.q: Which follows the docstring convention?
quiz.why: A triple-quoted string as the first statement is the documented convention.

challenge.prompt: Fill in the blank to print the function's docstring:
challenge.code:
def add(a, b):
    """Add a and b."""
    return a + b
print(____)
challenge.hint: Docstrings live in the __doc__ attribute.

lessons.title: The random Module: Build a Guessing Game
lessons.explain: The random module adds unpredictability: randint(a, b) picks an integer in a range, choice(seq) picks one item, and shuffle() mixes a list in place. Together they're all you need for games and simulations.
takeaways: `random.randint(1, 10)` can return 1 AND 10 — both ends are included.
`random.choice(['a', 'b'])` picks one item from a sequence.
`random.shuffle(deck)` shuffles in place and returns None.
lessons.code:
import random
print(random.randint(1, 6))
print(random.choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"]))
deck = [1, 2, 3]
random.shuffle(deck)
print(deck)

quiz.q: What values can `random.randint(1, 3)` return?
quiz.why: randint includes BOTH endpoints, unlike range().

quiz.q: What does `random.shuffle(cards)` return?
options: None — it shuffles the list in place
quiz.why: shuffle() mutates the list directly and returns None.

quiz.q: Which picks one random item from a list?
quiz.why: choice() is the real function; the others don't exist.

challenge.prompt: What will this print? (seed() makes randomness repeatable)
challenge.code:
import random
random.seed(42)
x = random.randint(1, 10)
random.seed(42)
y = random.randint(1, 10)
print(x == y)
challenge.hint: Same seed, same 'random' numbers.

lessons.title: Dates & Times with datetime
lessons.explain: The datetime module handles dates and times: date.today() gives you today, timedelta does date arithmetic like '7 days from now', and strftime() formats a date into any string layout you like.
takeaways: `from datetime import date, timedelta`, then `date.today()` is today's date.
Add `timedelta(days=7)` to a date to jump a week forward.
`strftime('%d %b %Y')` formats a date like '03 Nov 2026'.
lessons.code:
from datetime import date, timedelta
today = date.today()
print(today)
print(today + timedelta(days=7))

quiz.q: What does `date.today() + timedelta(days=1)` give?
quiz.why: Adding a one-day timedelta moves the date one day forward.

quiz.q: What type of object does `date.today()` return?
quiz.why: It returns a date object, which you can format or do math with.

quiz.q: How many days are in `timedelta(weeks=2)`?
quiz.why: weeks=2 is converted to 14 days internally.

challenge.code:
from datetime import date
print(date(2026, 1, 1).strftime("%A"))
challenge.hint: %A is the full weekday name — New Year's Day 2026 is a Thursday.

lessons.title: None & Checking for Nothing
lessons.explain: None is Python's way of saying 'no value here' — it's also what every function returns when it doesn't return anything. Always check for it with `is None`, never with `==`, because `is` tests identity.
takeaways: `None` means 'no value'; a function without return gives back None.
Check with `is None` / `is not None` — not `==`.
`None` is falsy, so `if result:` catches it too — but `is None` is explicit.
lessons.code:
def find_user(name):
    return None
user = find_user("ada")
print(user is None)
print(user)

quiz.q: What does this return? `def f():` followed by `x = 1` (no return statement)
quiz.why: A function without return always gives back None.

quiz.q: Which is the correct None check?
quiz.why: is tests identity, which is the reliable way to check for None.

quiz.q: What is `bool(None)`?
quiz.why: None is falsy, like 0 and empty collections.

challenge.code:
x = None
print(x is None)
challenge.hint: is checks identity — x really is None.

lessons.title: Comments & Clean Code Style
lessons.explain: Comments (#) explain WHY your code does something, not what — the code already says what. Clean style (clear names, blank lines between ideas, short lines) makes code readable for humans, including future you.
takeaways: Write comments for the WHY, not the WHAT: `# retry: the API is flaky`.
Use descriptive names (`total_price`) over cryptic ones (`tp`).
Python ignores everything after `#` on a line — handy for quick experiments.
lessons.code:
# convert minutes into hours and leftover minutes
mins = 135
hours = mins // 60
left = mins % 60
print(hours, left)

quiz.q: Which comment is most useful?
options: # retry 3 times: the API is flaky on weekends
quiz.why: It explains WHY the code exists — the code itself already shows the what.

quiz.q: What does Python do with text after `#`?
quiz.why: Everything from # to the end of the line is a comment.

quiz.q: Which variable name is cleanest?
quiz.why: Descriptive names read like English and need no decoding.

challenge.code:
print("a")
# print("b")
print("c")
challenge.hint: Lines starting with # never run.

lessons.title: Reading Tracebacks: Debugging Basics
lessons.explain: When Python crashes it prints a traceback — read it BOTTOM-UP. The last line names the error (like NameError or TypeError), and the lines above show exactly where it happened. Most bugs are found in seconds once you read tracebacks this way.
takeaways: Read tracebacks bottom-up: the LAST line is the actual error.
`NameError` = misspelled or undefined name; `TypeError` = wrong kind of operation.
The `line N` part pinpoints exactly where it broke.

quiz.q: Where is the most useful line of a traceback?
options: The last line — it names the error
quiz.why: The final line states the error type and message; work upward from there.

quiz.q: What error does `print(5 + 'a')` raise?
quiz.why: Adding an int and a str is an operation on the wrong types.

quiz.q: What error does `print(x)` raise if x was never defined?
quiz.why: Using a name that doesn't exist is a NameError.

challenge.hint: Index 5 doesn't exist in a 2-item list, so IndexError is raised and caught.

lessons.title: Capstone: Command-Line To-Do App
lessons.explain: Time to put it all together: a to-do app using a list of dictionaries, one function per action, and a loop for the menu. This is how small real programs are structured — data plus functions plus a main loop.
takeaways: Model each to-do as a dict (`{'task': ..., 'done': False}`) inside a list.
One function per action (add, list, complete) keeps the program organized.
A `while True` loop with `break` on 'quit' is the classic menu pattern.
lessons.code:
todos = []

def add(task):
    todos.append({"task": task, "done": False})

add("Study Python")
add("Build app")
todos[0]["done"] = True
print(len(todos), "tasks,", sum(1 for t in todos if t["done"]), "done")

quiz.q: How is each to-do stored in the capstone app?
options: As a dict inside a list
quiz.why: Each to-do is a dict with 'task' and 'done' keys, collected in a list.

quiz.q: How does the menu loop exit?
options: break when the user chooses quit
quiz.why: The classic pattern is `while True` with `break` on the quit choice.

quiz.q: Why write one function per action?
options: Each piece is testable and readable on its own
quiz.why: Small functions are easier to understand, test, and reuse.

challenge.prompt: How many tasks are done here?
challenge.code:
tasks = [{"t": "a", "done": True}, {"t": "b", "done": False}]
print(sum(1 for t in tasks if t["done"]))
challenge.hint: Only one dict has done set to True.

lessons.title: F-strings in Depth: Formatting Numbers & Dates
lessons.explain: An f-string can do more than drop a variable into text: a format spec after a colon controls decimals, commas, and percentages. You can even format a date inside the same f-string, so one line builds a tidy message like a receipt or a report.
takeaways: `f'{price:.2f}'` shows a number with exactly 2 decimal places — perfect for money.
`f'{big:,}'` adds thousand separators: `1234567` becomes `1,234,567`.
`f'{share:.1%}'` turns `0.256` into `25.6%` — the format multiplies by 100 for you.
Dates format with `strftime`, e.g. `date(2026, 11, 5).strftime('%d %b %Y')` gives `05 Nov 2026`.
lessons.code:
price = 49.99
print(f"Price: ${price:.2f}")
print(f"Big number: {1234567:,}")
print(f"Share: {0.256:.1%}")
from datetime import date
print(date(2026, 11, 5).strftime("%d %b %Y"))

quiz.q: What does `f'{3.14159:.2f}'` produce?
quiz.why: .2f rounds the number to exactly 2 decimal places.

quiz.q: What does `f'{1000000:,}'` produce?
quiz.why: The comma in the format spec adds thousand separators.

quiz.q: In `date(2026, 11, 5).strftime('%Y')`, what does `%Y` give?
quiz.why: %Y is the four-digit year, so it gives '2026'.

challenge.hint: The comma adds separators and .2f rounds to 2 decimal places.

lessons.title: String Building: join() vs + in Loops
lessons.explain: You can glue strings together with + or with join(), but they are not equal in a loop. Each + makes a brand-new string and copies everything again, while join() builds the final string in one pass — so for lists of words, join() is both tidier and faster.
takeaways: `', '.join(words)` puts the separator BETWEEN items, not after the last one.
`''.join(parts)` glues with no separator at all.
In a loop, prefer collecting pieces in a list and joining once over `result += piece` each time.
`join()` only works on strings — convert numbers with `str()` first.
lessons.code:
words = ["Ava", "Bo", "Al"]
print(" | ".join(words))
parts = []
for name in words:
    parts.append(name.upper())
print(" ".join(parts))

quiz.q: What does `', '.join(['a', 'b'])` return?
quiz.why: join() places the separator ', ' between the two items.

quiz.q: Why is join() better than `+` inside a loop?
options: Because + is slower only for lists
Because join() only works on numbers
Because join() builds the string in one pass instead of copying it on every +
Because + does not work on strings
quiz.why: Each + copies the whole string so far; join() assembles the pieces once.

quiz.q: What does `''.join(['p', 'y'])` return?
quiz.why: An empty separator glues the pieces directly together.

challenge.hint: join() puts the separator between the items.

lessons.title: Working with User Input: Validation Basics
lessons.explain: Input from a user always arrives as a string, and users type surprises — spaces, letters, or nothing at all. Before you trust it, tidy it with strip() and check it with isdigit(), so a bad answer gets a friendly retry instead of a crash.
takeaways: `input()` always returns a string, even when the user types digits.
`strip()` removes spaces from both ends: `'  27 '.strip()` is `'27'`.
`'42'.isdigit()` is True, but `'twenty'.isdigit()` is False — use it to check before converting.
Only call `int()` after the check passes, or a bad value raises a `ValueError`.
lessons.code:
raw = "  27 "
clean = raw.strip()
print(clean.isdigit())
print(int(clean) + 3)
bad = "twenty"
print(bad.isdigit())
print("Age OK" if clean.isdigit() else "Try again")

quiz.q: What does `'42'.isdigit()` return?
quiz.why: The string holds only digits, so isdigit() is True.

quiz.q: What does `strip()` do to a string?
options: Splits the text into a list
Returns True or False about digits
Converts the text to an integer
quiz.why: strip() trims spaces (and other whitespace) from the start and end only.

quiz.q: What happens when you run `int('12a')`?
quiz.why: '12a' is not a plain number, so int() raises a ValueError.

challenge.code: print("  9 ".strip())
challenge.hint: strip() trims the spaces from both ends.

lessons.title: Numbers: Rounding, abs, min/max in Practice
lessons.explain: Real programs rarely want a raw number — they want it rounded, made positive, or picked from a group. round() trims decimals, abs() drops the minus sign, and min() / max() pick the smallest or largest value, which covers most everyday number jobs.
takeaways: `round(3.14159, 2)` is `3.14` — the second argument is how many decimals to keep.
`abs(-7)` is `7`: abs() gives the distance from zero, ignoring the sign.
`min()` and `max()` take several values or a list: `max(4, 9, 2)` is `9`.
`round()` with no second argument returns a whole number, e.g. `round(3.6)` is `4`.
lessons.code:
print(round(3.14159, 2))
print(round(16.789, 1))
print(abs(-7))
print(min(4, 9, 2))
print(max(4, 9, 2))

quiz.q: What is `round(2.718, 1)`?
quiz.why: Rounding to 1 decimal place keeps the 7, since the next digit is 1.

quiz.q: What is `abs(-12)`?
quiz.why: abs() drops the sign, so -12 becomes 12.

quiz.q: What is `min([5, 3, 8])`?
quiz.why: min() picks the smallest value in the list, which is 3.

challenge.code: print(max(3, 11, 7))
challenge.hint: max() picks the largest of the three.

lessons.title: Comparisons & Chaining Conditions
lessons.explain: Python lets you chain comparisons the way you would say them out loud: `18 <= age < 65` means age is at least 18 AND under 65. The chain is just a neat shortcut for two comparisons joined by and, and it reads far more clearly.
takeaways: `18 <= age < 65` checks both sides at once — it means `18 <= age and age < 65`.
Every link in the chain must be True for the whole thing to be True.
`==` compares values; `=` assigns a value — mixing them up is a classic bug.
Chained comparisons work with any values you can compare, like scores or temperatures.
lessons.code:
age = 25
print(18 <= age < 65)
score = 85
print(80 <= score <= 100)
print(1 < 2 < 3)

quiz.q: What is the value of `5 < 8 < 10`?
quiz.why: Both 5 < 8 and 8 < 10 are True, so the chain is True.

quiz.q: What is the value of `10 <= 10`?
quiz.why: <= means 'less than or equal to', and 10 equals 10.

quiz.q: Which checks that age is between 13 and 19, including both ends?
quiz.why: <= on both sides includes 13 and 19 themselves.

challenge.hint: Both parts of the chain must be true — check each one.

lessons.title: Truthiness: What Counts as False?
lessons.explain: In an if statement, Python treats more than just False as false. Zero, empty strings, empty lists, empty dicts, and None all count as False — everything else counts as True. Once you know the list, you can write short checks like `if names:` instead of `if len(names) > 0:`.
takeaways: Falsy values: `False`, `0`, `0.0`, `''`, `[]`, `{}`, and `None` — everything else is truthy.
`bool()` shows the truth value: `bool('')` is False, `bool('hi')` is True.
`if names:` is the idiomatic way to check a list is not empty.
Watch out: `[0]` is truthy, because the list is not empty — only the empty list is falsy.
lessons.code:
print(bool(0))
print(bool(""))
print(bool([]))
print(bool("hi"))
print(bool([0]))

quiz.q: Which of these is falsy?
quiz.why: Zero counts as False; the others are all truthy.

quiz.q: What is `bool('False')`?
quiz.why: It is a non-empty string, and any non-empty string is truthy.

quiz.q: What is `bool([])`?
quiz.why: An empty list is falsy, so bool() gives False.

challenge.code: print(bool(""))
challenge.hint: An empty string counts as False.

lessons.title: while Loops: Sentinels & Menus
lessons.explain: A while loop is perfect when you do not know how many rounds you need — like a menu that repeats until the user picks quit. A sentinel is a special value, such as 'done' or 0, that means stop, and the loop keeps going until it shows up.
takeaways: A sentinel is an agreed stop value, e.g. `'done'` or `0`, that ends the loop.
A while loop repeats while its condition is True — check the sentinel in the condition.
Always move toward the sentinel inside the loop, or the loop never ends.
Menus use the same pattern: show options, read a choice, repeat until the choice is quit.
lessons.code:
entries = ["5", "9", "done"]
total = 0
idx = 0
while entries[idx] != "done":
    total += int(entries[idx])
    idx += 1
print(total)

quiz.q: What is a sentinel value?
options: A special value that signals the loop to stop
The first item in the list
quiz.why: The sentinel is the agreed value that tells the loop it is time to stop.

quiz.q: In a menu loop, when does the loop stop if the sentinel is 'quit'?
options: It never stops on its own
When the input is a number
quiz.why: The loop condition checks for the sentinel, so it stops on 'quit'.

quiz.q: What happens if the sentinel value never appears?
options: Python raises an error at once
quiz.why: With no sentinel and no other exit, the while condition stays True forever.

challenge.code:
x = 0
while x < 3:
    x += 1
print(x)
challenge.hint: The loop stops as soon as x reaches 3.

lessons.title: for Loops over Dictionaries
lessons.explain: A dictionary holds pairs of keys and values, and a for loop can walk through them in three ways. Looping directly gives you the keys, .values() gives you the values, and .items() gives you both at once — which is the one you will reach for most.
takeaways: `for key in scores:` loops over the keys only.
`for name, score in scores.items():` unpacks each key and value together.
`.keys()` and `.values()` give you just the keys or just the values.
Dictionary order follows insertion order — items come out in the order you added them.

quiz.q: What does `for k in my_dict:` loop over?
quiz.why: Looping a dictionary directly yields its keys, one at a time.

quiz.q: What does `.items()` give you?
quiz.why: items() yields each key together with its value as a pair.

quiz.q: If `scores = {'Ava': 9, 'Bo': 7}`, what does `scores.values()` hold?
quiz.why: values() gives the values, 9 and 7, without the keys.

challenge.code:
for k in {"a": 1, "b": 2}:
    print(k)
challenge.hint: Looping over a dictionary gives you its keys.

lessons.title: List Comprehension: A Gentle First Look
lessons.explain: A list comprehension builds a new list in a single line: `[n * n for n in nums]` reads as 'give me n squared for every n in nums'. It does exactly what a small for loop with append() does, just more compactly — start with simple ones like this and the pattern will click.
takeaways: `[n * n for n in nums]` makes a NEW list; the original is unchanged.
Read it as: expression first, then the loop — `[n.upper() for n in names]`.
It replaces a loop that only appends to a list — nothing more, nothing less.
Keep comprehensions short; if the logic gets complicated, use a plain loop instead.
lessons.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
squares = [n * n for n in nums]
print(squares)
names = ["ava", "bo"]
print([n.upper() for n in names])

quiz.q: What is `[n * 2 for n in [1, 2, 3]]`?
quiz.why: Each item is doubled: 1 becomes 2, 2 becomes 4, 3 becomes 6.

quiz.q: What is a list comprehension, in plain words?
options: A loop that builds a new list in one line
A way to delete list items
quiz.why: It is shorthand for a loop that appends each result to a new list.

quiz.q: How many items are in `[x for x in [1, 2]]`?
quiz.why: One output item is produced for each input item, so there are 2.

challenge.code: print([x + 10 for x in [1, 2]])
challenge.hint: Each item gets 10 added to it.

lessons.title: Functions: Return vs Print
lessons.explain: Print and return look similar because both show you a value, but they do very different jobs. print() displays a value on the screen and then it is gone; return hands the value back to the caller, who can store it, compare it, or pass it on — which is what you want when a function computes an answer.
takeaways: `return a + b` hands the answer back; `print(a + b)` only shows it.
A function with no return gives back `None` — even if it printed something.
Use return when the caller needs the result; use print when a human needs to see it.
You can do both: return the value AND print a message about it.
lessons.code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b
print(add(2, 3))
def shout(word):
    print(word.upper())
result = shout("hi")
print(result)

quiz.q: What does a function give back if it has no return statement?
quiz.why: Python returns None automatically when a function ends without return.

quiz.q: What is the difference between print() and return inside a function?
options: print() stores the value in a variable
They do exactly the same thing
return prints the value on screen
print() shows a value; return hands it back so code can use it
quiz.why: print() is for humans to see; return is for the calling code to use.

quiz.q: If `add` returns `a + b`, what is `total = add(2, 3)`?
quiz.why: return hands 5 back, and the assignment stores it in total.

challenge.code:
def f():
    print("hi")
x = f()
print(x)
challenge.hint: f prints hi, but with no return it gives back None.

lessons.title: Functions: Passing Lists & Dicts
lessons.explain: When you pass a list or a dictionary to a function, the function receives the very same object — not a copy. So append() or an assignment inside the function changes the caller's data too. That is powerful, but you must do it on purpose, never by accident.
takeaways: Lists and dicts are passed by reference: the function sees the caller's object itself.
`scores.append(30)` inside a function changes the list outside it too.
Assigning a new value to a dict key inside a function also shows up outside.
Pass `my_list.copy()` when the function should work on its own copy.

quiz.q: A function appends to a list passed in as an argument. What happens to the list outside?
quiz.why: The function appends to the very same list object the caller passed in.

quiz.q: Why does the change show up outside the function?
options: Python copies every list before passing it
The function sees the very same list object
quiz.why: Lists are passed by reference, so caller and function share one object.

quiz.q: How do you pass a list so the function cannot change the original?
quiz.why: copy() makes a separate list, so appends inside the function stay local.

challenge.code:
def add(lst):
    lst.append(3)
a = [1, 2]
add(a)
print(a)
challenge.hint: append() changes the same list the caller passed in.

lessons.title: Default Arguments & the Mutable Default Trap
lessons.explain: Default arguments are handy, but there is a famous trap: a default list is created ONCE, when the function is defined, and every call without that argument shares the same list. Items from one call leak into the next — the fix is to default to None and build a fresh list inside.
takeaways: A default value is created once at definition time, not fresh on each call.
Sharing a default list makes calls leak into each other — the classic mutable default trap.
The fix: `def add(item, bag=None):` then `if bag is None: bag = []` inside.
Defaults like numbers and strings are safe, because they cannot be changed in place.
lessons.code:
def add_buggy(item, bag=[]):
    bag.append(item)
    return bag
print(add_buggy("a"))
print(add_buggy("b"))
def add_fixed(item, bag=None):
    if bag is None:
        bag = []
    bag.append(item)
    return bag
print(add_fixed("a"))
print(add_fixed("b"))

quiz.q: When is a default argument value created?
options: Once, when the function is defined
quiz.why: Python evaluates the default once at definition time and reuses it.

quiz.q: How do you fix the mutable default trap?
options: Use a tuple as the default
Use None as the default and create a fresh list inside
quiz.why: None is immutable, and a new list built inside the function is fresh each call.

quiz.q: After `print(add_buggy('a'))` then `print(add_buggy('b'))`, what does the second call return?
quiz.why: Both calls share the one default list, so 'a' is still in it.

challenge.code:
def f(x, bag=[]):
    bag.append(x)
    return bag
print(f(1))
print(f(2))
challenge.hint: The same default list is reused by both calls.

lessons.title: Errors You Will Meet: NameError, TypeError, IndexError
lessons.explain: Three errors show up in almost every beginner program, and each one points at a different mistake. NameError means you used a name Python has never seen, TypeError means the operation does not fit the types, and IndexError means you asked a list for a position that is not there.
takeaways: `NameError`: a name was never defined, or is misspelled — check the spelling.
`TypeError`: the operation does not work on those types, e.g. `10 + '5'`.
`IndexError`: the list index is out of range, e.g. `[1, 2][5]`.
Read the LAST line of the traceback first — it names the error and the line.

quiz.q: What error does `print(x)` raise if `x` was never defined?
quiz.why: Using a name that does not exist is a NameError.

quiz.q: What error does `[1, 2][5]` raise?
quiz.why: Index 5 is out of range for a 2-item list.

quiz.q: What error does `5 + 'a'` raise?
quiz.why: Adding an int and a str is an operation on the wrong types.

challenge.hint: unknown was never defined, so NameError is raised and caught.

lessons.title: The math Module: Everyday Helpers
lessons.explain: The math module is a small toolbox for numbers you will use constantly: sqrt() for square roots, ceil() and floor() for rounding up or down, and constants like pi. Import it once, and these helpers are ready whenever a calculation needs them.
takeaways: `math.sqrt(16)` is `4.0` — square roots always come back as floats.
`math.ceil(4.2)` is `5` (rounds up) and `math.floor(4.8)` is `4` (rounds down).
`math.pi` is 3.14159... — use it instead of typing 3.14 yourself.
Always `import math` first; the helpers live inside the module, not built in.
lessons.code:
import math
print(math.sqrt(16))
print(math.ceil(4.2))
print(math.floor(4.8))
print(round(math.pi, 2))

quiz.q: What is `math.sqrt(25)`?
quiz.why: sqrt() returns a float, so the square root of 25 is 5.0.

quiz.q: What is `math.ceil(3.1)`?
quiz.why: ceil() rounds UP to the next whole number, which is 4.

quiz.q: What is `math.pi` approximately?
quiz.why: pi is about 3.14159, so 3.14 is the closest choice.

challenge.code:
import math
print(math.floor(9.9))
challenge.hint: floor() always rounds down to the whole number below.

lessons.title: The string Module & Constants
lessons.explain: The string module holds ready-made constants so you never have to type the alphabet or the digits by hand. string.ascii_lowercase, string.ascii_uppercase, string.digits, and string.punctuation are the four you will use most — for validation, passwords, and text checks.
takeaways: `string.ascii_lowercase` is `'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz'`.
`string.digits` is `'0123456789'` and `string.punctuation` holds all the symbols.
`string.capwords('hello world')` gives `'Hello World'` — handy for tidying titles.
Use these constants instead of typing character lists yourself — fewer typos.
lessons.code:
import string
print(string.ascii_lowercase[:5])
print(string.digits)
print(string.punctuation[:4])
print(string.capwords("hello world"))

quiz.q: What is `string.digits`?
quiz.why: digits is the string of all ten decimal digits.

quiz.q: What does `string.ascii_uppercase` start with?
quiz.why: It is the uppercase alphabet, starting with A, B, C.

quiz.q: What is `string.capwords('hi there')`?
quiz.why: capwords() capitalizes the first letter of every word.

challenge.code:
import string
print(string.ascii_lowercase[0])
challenge.hint: The lowercase alphabet starts with a.

lessons.title: Guided Project: Number Guessing Game
lessons.explain: This project pulls together everything in the beginner track: a secret number, a loop over guesses, if/elif/else hints, and a break when the player wins. Follow the shape below, then make it yours — in the real game the secret comes from random.randint(1, 10) so every round is different.
takeaways: Pick the secret first — in the real game use `random.randint(1, 10)` for a fresh one each round.
Compare each guess: too low means guess higher, too high means guess lower.
`break` stops the loop the moment the player wins — no extra guesses.
Count tries as you go, so the win message can say how many guesses it took.

quiz.q: What makes the game different every time you play it?
options: Picking a fresh secret with random.randint(1, 10) each game
Printing the secret at the start
quiz.why: randint() picks a new secret number each game, so no two rounds are alike.

quiz.q: Why use `break` after the player guesses correctly?
options: To stop the loop once the game is won
quiz.why: The game is over, so break ends the loop instead of asking for more guesses.

quiz.q: A guess is smaller than the secret. What should the game say?
quiz.why: A smaller guess is too low, so the player should try a bigger number.

challenge.hint: The guess equals the secret, so the win branch runs.

lessons.title: Guided Project: Simple Quiz App
lessons.explain: A quiz app is a list of questions, a loop that asks each one, and a score that grows with every right answer. Store each question as a dictionary with the question text and its correct answer, then compare the player's answer with the stored one.
takeaways: Store each question as a dict like `{"question": ..., "answer": ...}` inside a list.
Loop over the questions and compare the player's answer with `q["answer"]`.
Keep a `score` counter and print it as `score/len(questions)` at the end.
lessons.code:
questions = [{"question": "What is 2 + 3?", "answer": "5"}, {"question": "Capital of France?", "answer": "Paris"}]
answers = ["5", "London"]
score = 0
for q, a in zip(questions, answers):
    if a == q["answer"]:
        score += 1
print(f"Score: {score}/{len(questions)}")

quiz.q: How should you store the questions in a quiz app?
options: A single string with all questions joined together
A list of dicts, one per question with its answer
quiz.why: Each question needs its text and its correct answer together, so a list of dicts is the natural fit.

quiz.q: If a player answers 2 of 3 questions correctly, what is the score?
quiz.why: The score counts correct answers, and 2 of the 3 were right.

quiz.q: Why compare the player's answer with the stored answer?
options: To make the program run faster
To decide whether the answer is correct and add to the score
To delete the question from the list
quiz.why: The comparison is the check itself: a match means the answer was right.

challenge.code:
questions = [{"question": "What is 2 + 2?", "answer": "4"}, {"question": "Capital of France?", "answer": "Paris"}]
answers = ["4", "Paris"]
score = sum(1 for q, a in zip(questions, answers) if a == q["answer"])
print(f"{score}/{len(questions)}")
challenge.hint: Both answers match their stored answers, so both count.

lessons.title: Guided Project: Rock, Paper, Scissors
lessons.explain: Rock, Paper, Scissors is a small game with three rules: rock beats scissors, scissors beats paper, and paper beats rock. The computer picks with random.choice(), and a helper function decides the winner from the two choices.
takeaways: `random.choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"])` picks the computer's move.
A `winner(you, computer)` function keeps the rules in one place instead of scattered ifs.
Check for a draw first, then the three winning pairs, and let anything else mean the computer wins.
lessons.code:
import random

def winner(you, computer):
    if you == computer:
        return "Draw!"
    if (you, computer) in [("rock", "scissors"), ("paper", "rock"), ("scissors", "paper")]:
        return "You win!"
    return "Computer wins!"

random.seed(3)
you = "rock"
computer = random.choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"])
print("You:", you)
print("Computer:", computer)
print(winner(you, computer))

quiz.q: Which move beats rock?
quiz.why: Paper covers rock, so paper beats rock.

quiz.q: How does the computer pick its move?
options: With random.choice() from the three moves
quiz.why: choice() picks one item from the list of moves at random.

quiz.q: What should the winner function return when both players pick paper?
quiz.why: Equal moves are a draw, so that check comes first.

challenge.hint: Paper covers rock — which of the three winning pairs is that?

lessons.title: Guided Project: Password Generator
lessons.explain: A password generator builds a string by picking random characters, one at a time, from a pool of letters and digits. random.choice() picks one character, and a loop (or a short comprehension) repeats that for the length you want.
takeaways: `string.ascii_letters + string.digits` is a handy pool of characters to pick from.
`random.choice(pool)` picks one random character; repeat it to build the password.
`"".join(...)` glues the picked characters into a single string.
lessons.code:
import random
import string

random.seed(7)
chars = string.ascii_letters + string.digits
password = "".join(random.choice(chars) for _ in range(8))
print(password)
print(len(password))

quiz.q: What does `random.choice(chars)` return?
quiz.why: choice() picks exactly one item from the sequence you give it.

quiz.q: How do you turn 8 picked characters into one password string?
quiz.why: join() glues the characters together with no separator between them.

quiz.q: What is `len(password)` if the password was built with `range(8)`?
quiz.why: range(8) picks exactly 8 characters, so the password is 8 long.

challenge.code:
import random
import string
random.seed(7)
password = "".join(random.choice(string.ascii_letters) for _ in range(10))
print(len(password))
challenge.hint: Count how many times the loop picks a character.

lessons.title: Guided Project: Simple Calculator with Functions
lessons.explain: A calculator is cleaner when each operation is its own small function: add, subtract, multiply and divide each take two numbers and return the result. The main code then just calls the right function instead of repeating arithmetic everywhere.
takeaways: One small function per operation (`add`, `subtract`, `multiply`, `divide`) keeps the calculator organised.
Each function should `return` its result so the caller can print it or use it further.
Calling `divide(6, 3)` gives `2.0` because `/` always returns a float.

quiz.q: Why write a separate function for each operation?
options: So each operation is named, testable and reusable
quiz.why: Small named functions are easier to understand, test and reuse than repeated arithmetic.

quiz.q: What does `divide(6, 3)` return?
quiz.why: The / operator always returns a float, even when the result is a whole number.

quiz.q: What happens if a calculator function uses `print` instead of `return`?
options: The caller cannot use the result in further maths
quiz.why: print only shows the value; return hands it back so the caller can store or combine it.

challenge.hint: multiply returns a times b — work out 3 times 4.

lessons.title: Guided Project: Word Counter Script
lessons.explain: A word counter turns text into a list of words with split(), then counts them. len(words) is the total, len(set(words)) is the number of unique words, and words.count("python") tells you how often one word appears.
takeaways: `text.split()` breaks text into a list of words, splitting on whitespace.
`len(words)` is the total word count; `len(set(words))` counts unique words.
`words.count("python")` counts how many times one word appears — lower the text first so "Python" and "python" match.
lessons.code:
text = "Python is fun and Python is useful"
words = text.lower().split()
print("Words:", len(words))
print("Unique:", len(set(words)))
print("Python appears:", words.count("python"))

quiz.q: What does `"hello world".split()` return?
quiz.why: split() cuts the string at whitespace into a list of two words.

quiz.q: How do you count the unique words in a list called `words`?
quiz.why: A set drops duplicates, so its length is the number of distinct words.

quiz.q: Why call `.lower()` before counting the word "python"?
options: So "Python" and "python" count as the same word
quiz.why: Without lowercasing, "Python" and "python" are different strings and would be counted separately.

challenge.code:
text = "one two two three"
words = text.split()
print(len(set(words)))
challenge.hint: The set drops the repeated word — how many distinct words are left?

lessons.title: Working with Dates: Birthdays & Deadlines
lessons.explain: Subtracting one date from another gives a timedelta, and its .days tells you how many days are between them — perfect for counting down to a birthday or an exam. strftime() then formats a date into a readable string like '20 Nov 2026'.
takeaways: `date(2026, 11, 20) - date(2026, 11, 5)` is a timedelta; `.days` gives 15.
`date.today()` gives today's real date; use it instead of a fixed date in real programs.
`birthday.strftime("%d %b %Y")` formats a date as '20 Nov 2026'.
lessons.code:
from datetime import date
today = date(2026, 11, 5)
birthday = date(2026, 11, 20)
print("Days until birthday:", (birthday - today).days)
deadline = date(2026, 11, 12)
print("Days until exam:", (deadline - today).days)
print(birthday.strftime("%d %b %Y"))

quiz.why: 10 November is 5 days after 5 November.

quiz.q: What does `date.today()` return?
options: Today's date as a date object
The number of days in the month
quiz.why: It returns a date object for today, which you can format or do maths with.

quiz.q: What does `date(2026, 11, 20).strftime("%d %b %Y")` produce?
quiz.why: %d is the day, %b the short month name, and %Y the four-digit year.

challenge.code:
from datetime import date
print((date(2026, 11, 10) - date(2026, 11, 5)).days)
challenge.hint: Count the days from the 5th to the 10th.

lessons.title: Time Delays & Timers with time
lessons.explain: time.sleep(seconds) pauses your program for that long — handy for countdowns, retries and rate limits. time.time() returns the current time as a number of seconds, so subtracting a start time from an end time tells you how long something took.
takeaways: `time.sleep(0.2)` pauses the program for about 0.2 seconds.
`time.time()` returns seconds since 1970; `end - start` is the elapsed time.
`time.sleep()` returns None — it pauses, it does not give you a value.
lessons.code:
import time
start = time.time()
print("Start")
time.sleep(0.2)
print("End")
print("Elapsed:", round(time.time() - start, 1))

quiz.q: What does `time.sleep(1)` do?
options: Pauses the program for about 1 second
quiz.why: sleep() waits for the given number of seconds, then lets the program continue.

quiz.q: How do you measure how long a piece of code took?
options: Record time.time() before and after, then subtract
quiz.why: The difference between the two timestamps is the elapsed time.

quiz.q: What does `time.sleep(0.2)` return?
quiz.why: sleep() only pauses; like most functions that just do something, it returns None.

challenge.code:
import time
print(time.sleep(0.1) is None)
challenge.hint: sleep() pauses and returns nothing — what does a function that returns nothing give back?

lessons.title: Command-Line Arguments Basics (sys.argv)
lessons.explain: When you run `python greet.py Ava`, Python puts the words after the script name into sys.argv — a list where argv[0] is the script's own name and argv[1] is the first real argument. Always check len(sys.argv) before reading argv[1], or the program crashes when run with no arguments.
takeaways: `sys.argv` is a list of the words typed after `python script.py`.
`sys.argv[0]` is the script name; the first real argument is `sys.argv[1]`.
Guard with `if len(sys.argv) > 1` and fall back to a default when no argument was given.
lessons.code:
import sys
name = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "friend"
print(f"Hello, {name}!")
print("Arguments:", len(sys.argv))

quiz.q: If you run `python greet.py Ava`, what is `sys.argv[1]`?
quiz.why: argv[0] is the script name, so argv[1] is the first argument after it.

quiz.q: What is `sys.argv[0]`?
quiz.why: Python always puts the script filename in argv[0].

quiz.q: What happens if you read `sys.argv[1]` when the program was run with no arguments?
quiz.why: With no arguments the list has only argv[0], so index 1 does not exist.

challenge.prompt: What will this print when run with NO arguments?
challenge.code:
import sys
name = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "guest"
print(name)
challenge.hint: With no arguments, len(sys.argv) is 1 — so which branch runs?

lessons.title: Environment Variables & Secrets Basics
lessons.explain: Environment variables are settings that live outside your code — like which mode your app runs in — so the same code behaves differently on your laptop and on a server. Secrets like API keys belong there too, never written into your code, because code gets shared and secrets must not.
takeaways: `os.environ.get("APP_MODE", "development")` reads a setting, falling back to "development" if it is not set.
Never hard-code a secret in your code — read it from an environment variable instead.
`"MY_API_KEY" in os.environ` tells you whether a variable is set at all.
lessons.code:
import os
mode = os.environ.get("APP_MODE", "development")
print("Mode:", mode)
print("Has API key:", "MY_API_KEY" in os.environ)

quiz.q: What does `os.environ.get("APP_MODE", "development")` return when APP_MODE is not set?
quiz.why: get() returns the default you supplied when the variable is missing.

quiz.q: Where should an API key live?
options: In an environment variable, outside the code
Hard-coded at the top of the file
quiz.why: Code gets shared and published; a key in the code leaks the moment it does.

quiz.q: How do you check whether a variable called MY_API_KEY is set?
quiz.why: os.environ behaves like a dict, so `in` tests whether the key exists.

challenge.code:
import os
print(os.environ.get("DOES_NOT_EXIST", "fallback"))
challenge.hint: The variable is not set, so get() returns the second argument.

lessons.title: Debugging with print(): A Systematic Approach
lessons.explain: Debugging with print() means placing prints on purpose: one before a suspicious step showing the inputs, and one after showing the result. When the printed values stop matching what you expected, you have found the exact line where things went wrong.
takeaways: Print the INPUTS before a step and the RESULT after it, so you can see where they diverge.
Print inside a loop to watch a value change each round — `print("total so far:", total)`.
Narrow down first, then fix: a print that shows the wrong value halfway through beats guessing at the end.

quiz.q: Where is the most useful place for a debug print?
options: Only at the very end of the program
Before and after the suspicious step, showing inputs and results
quiz.why: Seeing both sides of a step shows exactly where the value first goes wrong.

quiz.q: What does printing inside a loop help you see?
options: How a value changes on each round
The number of lines in the file
quiz.why: One print per round gives you a trace of the value over time.

quiz.q: Your print shows the total is wrong after the third loop round. What next?
options: Fix the code inside that round — that is where it went wrong
quiz.why: The first round where the value goes wrong pinpoints the faulty step.

challenge.hint: 10 // 2 is floor division — work out 10 divided by 2, rounded down.

lessons.title: Code Style: Naming Things Well
lessons.explain: A good name says what a value IS, so the code reads like a sentence: total_price and final_price need no explanation, while tp and x do. Pick names that are specific, use full words, and say what the thing means — not what type it is.
takeaways: Name values by MEANING: `total_price` beats `tp`, and `final_price` beats `x`.
Use full words and underscores: `item_count`, not `ic` or `itemcount`.
A clear name is documentation — if you need a comment to explain a name, rename it.
lessons.code:
total_price = 120
discount = 20
final_price = total_price - discount
print("Final price:", final_price)

quiz.q: Which variable name is clearest for a shopping total?
quiz.why: total_price says exactly what the value is, with no decoding needed.

quiz.q: Why are single-letter names like `x` usually a bad choice?
options: They make the code run slower
They say nothing about what the value means
quiz.why: A name's job is to explain the value; x explains nothing.

quiz.q: What should you do if a name needs a comment to explain it?
options: Rename it so the name explains itself
Keep the name and add a longer comment
quiz.why: A good name is its own documentation — renaming fixes the real problem.

challenge.code:
item_count = 3
price_per_item = 10
print(item_count * price_per_item)
challenge.hint: 3 items at 10 each — multiply them.

lessons.title: Capstone: Personal Expense Tracker
lessons.explain: An expense tracker is a list of dictionaries — each expense has an item, an amount and a category — plus a few sums: total spent, and totals per category. sum() with a generator expression does the adding in one line, and a filter (if e["category"] == "food") narrows it to one category.
takeaways: Each expense is a dict (`{"item": ..., "amount": ..., "category": ...}`) in a list.
`sum(e["amount"] for e in expenses)` adds up every expense in one line.
Add `if e["category"] == "food"` inside the sum to total just one category.
lessons.code:
expenses = [{"item": "Lunch", "amount": 150, "category": "food"}, {"item": "Bus", "amount": 40, "category": "travel"}, {"item": "Book", "amount": 200, "category": "study"}]
total = sum(e["amount"] for e in expenses)
print("Total spent:", total)
print("Food total:", sum(e["amount"] for e in expenses if e["category"] == "food"))

quiz.q: How is each expense stored in this tracker?
options: As a dict with item, amount and category
quiz.why: Each expense needs its item, amount and category together, so a dict is the fit.

quiz.q: What is the total of expenses 150, 40 and 200?
How do you total only the food expenses?
options: sum(e["amount"] for e in expenses if e["category"] == "food")
quiz.why: The if inside the generator keeps only food expenses before adding them up.

challenge.code:
expenses = [{"amount": 100}, {"amount": 50}]
print(sum(e["amount"] for e in expenses))
challenge.hint: Add the two amounts together.

lessons.title: Capstone: Flashcard Quiz App
lessons.explain: A flashcard app is the quiz idea taken one step further: each card is a dictionary with a question and an answer, the app shows the question, checks the answer, and reports the score. The same list-of-dicts pattern you used for quizzes and expenses powers this whole app.
takeaways: Each flashcard is a dict (`{"question": ..., "answer": ...}`) in a list.
Compare each answer with the card's stored answer and count the matches.
The same pattern — list of dicts, loop, compare, score — builds quizzes, flashcards and trackers.
lessons.code:
cards = [{"question": "What is 2 + 2?", "answer": "4"}, {"question": "Capital of France?", "answer": "Paris"}, {"question": "What is 5 * 3?", "answer": "15"}]
answers = ["4", "London", "15"]
score = sum(1 for c, a in zip(cards, answers) if a == c["answer"])
print(f"You got {score}/{len(cards)} right")

quiz.q: How is one flashcard stored?
options: As a dict with a question and an answer
quiz.why: Each card pairs its question with its correct answer, so a dict is the natural fit.

quiz.q: With answers ["4", "London", "15"] against cards 2+2=4, Paris, 5*3=15, what is the score?
quiz.why: Two answers match (4 and 15); London is wrong for Paris.

quiz.q: What pattern do the quiz app, flashcard app and expense tracker share?
options: A list of dicts, a loop, and a summary at the end
quiz.why: All three store records as dicts in a list, loop over them, and summarise the result.

challenge.code:
cards = [{"question": "What is 2 + 2?", "answer": "4"}]
answers = ["4"]
score = sum(1 for c, a in zip(cards, answers) if a == c["answer"])
print(f"{score}/{len(cards)}")
challenge.hint: The one answer matches the one stored answer.

lessons.title: Functions & Return Values
lessons.explain: Functions package reusable logic under a name. def defines one, parameters receive input, and return sends a result back to the caller. Default parameters (like greeting="Hello") make arguments optional — callers can skip them.
takeaways: def name(params): defines a function; call it with name(args).
return sends a value back. Without it, a function returns None.
Default parameters make arguments optional.
lessons.code:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}!"

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

print(greet("Vikas"))
print(greet("Sara", greeting="Welcome"))
print("Sum:", add(7, 5))

quiz.q: What does return do?
options: Sends a value back to the caller
quiz.why: return hands a value back to whoever called the function; print just displays it.

quiz.q: In def greet(name, greeting="Hello"), greeting is…
quiz.why: It has a default value, so callers may omit it.

quiz.q: What does this print? def add(a, b): return a + b, then print(add(2, 3))
quiz.why: add(2, 3) returns 5, which print displays.

quiz.q: What does a function without return give back?
quiz.why: Falling off the end of a function returns None.

quiz.q: What does this print? def greet(name, greeting="Hello"): return greeting + " " + name, then print(greet("Sam"))
quiz.why: greeting falls back to its default, "Hello".

challenge.hint: b isn't given, so the default 10 is used: 5 + 10.

lessons.title: List Methods in Depth
lessons.explain: Lists are mutable, and their methods change them in place. append() adds one item to the end, extend() adds many, insert() squeezes one in at a position, remove() deletes by value, and pop() takes an item out and hands it back.
takeaways: `append()` adds ONE item; `extend()` adds EACH item of another list.
`pop()` removes AND returns an item; `remove()` deletes by value.
Most list methods return None — the change happens to the list itself.
lessons.code:
nums = [1, 2]
nums.append(3)
nums.extend([4, 5])
print(nums)
print(nums.pop())
print(nums)

quiz.q: After `a = [1, 2]` and `a.append([3, 4])`, what is `a`?
quiz.why: append() adds its argument as a single item, so the list becomes nested.

quiz.q: What does `[10, 20, 30].pop(0)` return?
quiz.why: pop(0) removes and returns the item at index 0, which is 10.

quiz.q: Which removes the FIRST occurrence of the value 5 from `lst`?
quiz.why: remove() deletes by value; pop() works by index instead.

challenge.code:
a = [10, 20]
a.append(30)
print(len(a))
challenge.hint: len() counts items, and append() added one more.

lessons.title: Tuples: Unpacking & Immutability
lessons.explain: A tuple is like a list you can't change — perfect for fixed data like coordinates or RGB colors. You can unpack a tuple into separate variables in one line, which makes swaps and multiple values elegant.
takeaways: Tuples are immutable: you can't add, remove, or change items after creation.
Unpacking assigns each item to its own variable: `x, y = (3, 4)`.
Use tuples for data that should never change, like coordinates or dates.
lessons.code:
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
print(x + y)
print((x, y))

quiz.q: What happens when you run `(1, 2).append(3)`?
options: It works just like a list
quiz.why: Tuples are immutable and have no append method at all.

quiz.q: After `a, b = (5, 9)`, what is `a + b`?
quiz.why: Unpacking gives a = 5 and b = 9, so a + b is 14.

quiz.q: Why choose a tuple over a list?
options: To protect data from accidental changes
Tuples are always faster to type
quiz.why: Immutability is a feature: it guarantees the data stays exactly as created.

challenge.code:
x, y = (10, 20)
print(y - x)
challenge.hint: After unpacking, y is 20 and x is 10.

lessons.title: Dictionary Methods in Depth
lessons.explain: Dictionaries store key-value pairs, and their methods make lookups safe and iteration easy. get() avoids KeyError crashes, keys()/values()/items() expose the contents, and update() merges another dictionary in.
takeaways: `d.get(key, default)` returns the default instead of crashing when a key is missing.
`d.items()` lets you loop over key AND value together: `for k, v in d.items()`.
`setdefault()` inserts a key only if it isn't already there.

quiz.q: What does `{}.get('x', 'none')` return?
quiz.why: The key is missing, so get() returns the default you supplied.

quiz.q: Which loop prints both keys and values of `d`?
quiz.why: items() yields (key, value) pairs, which unpack neatly into k and v.

quiz.q: After `d = {'a': 1}` and `d.update({'b': 2})`, what is `d`?
quiz.why: update() merges the new pairs into the existing dictionary.

challenge.code:
d = {"x": 1}
print(d.get("y"))
challenge.hint: get() without a default returns None for missing keys.

lessons.title: Set Operations: Union, Intersection & Difference
lessons.explain: Sets hold unique items and support math-style operations. Union (|) combines everything from both sets, intersection (&) keeps only what's in both, and difference (-) keeps what's only in the first.
takeaways: Sets automatically drop duplicates: `set([1, 1, 2])` is `{1, 2}`.
`a | b` is the union, `a & b` the intersection, `a - b` the difference.
Use a set for fast membership tests or to remove duplicates from a list.

quiz.why: Union combines all unique items from both sets.

quiz.q: What does `{1, 2, 3} & {2, 4}` give?
quiz.why: Intersection keeps only items present in BOTH sets — just 2.

quiz.q: What is `len(set([5, 5, 5, 6]))`?
quiz.why: Duplicates collapse, leaving {5, 6}, which has 2 items.

challenge.hint: Difference keeps the items NOT in the second set.

lessons.title: Dictionaries in Practice: Counting & Grouping
lessons.explain: Counting things is one of the most common jobs in programming — votes, words, survey answers — and a dictionary is the natural tool. Each distinct value becomes a key, and the value is how many times you have seen it, with .get() handling the first sighting safely.
takeaways: `counts.get(v, 0)` returns 0 for a key you have not seen yet, so no KeyError.
The counting pattern is: `counts[v] = counts.get(v, 0) + 1`.
Grouping works the same way: the key is the group name, the value is a list or a count.
After the loop, `counts['red']` tells you how many reds there were.

quiz.q: If `counts` has no key 'green', what is `counts.get('green', 0)`?
quiz.why: get() returns the fallback 0 when the key is missing.

quiz.q: Why use `.get(v, 0)` when counting?
options: It avoids a KeyError for a key seen the first time
It deletes the key after counting
It makes the count start at 1
quiz.why: The first sighting has no entry yet, and get() supplies 0 instead of crashing.

quiz.q: After counting `['red', 'blue', 'red', 'red', 'blue']`, what is `counts['blue']`?
quiz.why: 'blue' appears twice in the list.

challenge.hint: Count how many times the letter a appears in banana.

lessons.title: Sets in Practice: Deduplication
lessons.explain: A set is a collection that refuses to hold duplicates — add the same value twice and it simply stays once. That makes sets the quickest way to clean a list of repeats, or to check whether something has been seen before.
takeaways: `set([3, 1, 3, 2])` is `{1, 2, 3}` — duplicates are dropped automatically.
`len(set(items))` tells you how many DISTINCT values there are.
Sets are unordered, so sort the result with `sorted()` when order matters.
`'Ava' in my_set` is a fast membership check — use it instead of scanning a list.
lessons.code:
nums = [3, 1, 3, 2, 1, 3]
print(sorted(set(nums)))
print(len(set(nums)))
names = {"Ava", "Bo"}
print("Ava" in names)

quiz.q: What is `set([1, 1, 2])`?
quiz.why: A set keeps each value only once, so the duplicate 1 disappears.

quiz.q: Why use `sorted(set(...))` instead of just `set(...)`?
options: Sets keep their items in order anyway
Sets have no order, so sorting gives a tidy result
quiz.why: Set order is not guaranteed, so sorted() arranges the unique values neatly.

quiz.q: What is `len(set('hello'))`?
quiz.why: 'hello' has the distinct letters h, e, l, o — four in total.

challenge.hint: Duplicates collapse, so only the distinct values are counted.

lessons.title: Tuples in Practice: Returning Multiple Values
lessons.explain: A function can only return one thing — but that one thing can be a tuple holding several values. Return `min(nums), max(nums)` and the caller unpacks them into two variables in one line, which is how Python functions hand back a low and a high together.
