lessons.title: Error Handling with try/except
lessons.explain: Errors (exceptions) crash programs unless handled. Wrap risky code in try, catch specific problems with except, and use finally for cleanup that must always run. Handling specific errors beats a bare except — it keeps real bugs visible.
takeaways: try/except catches exceptions so your program survives them.
Catch specific errors (ZeroDivisionError) before general ones.
finally always runs — perfect for cleanup.

quiz.q: Without try/except, what happens on 10 / 0?
quiz.why: An unhandled exception terminates the program with a traceback.

quiz.q: A finally block…
quiz.why: finally executes whether or not an exception occurred.

quiz.q: What does this print? try: x = int("abc"), except ValueError: x = -1, then print(x)
quiz.why: int("abc") raises ValueError, which the except block catches.

quiz.q: Accessing a missing dict key raises…
quiz.why: Missing keys raise KeyError — catch that specifically.

quiz.q: What prints? try: print("a"), except: print("b"), else: print("c")
quiz.why: No error occurs, so try runs, then the else block runs.

challenge.hint: int("abc") raises ValueError, which the except catches.

lessons.title: Error Handling
lessons.explain: Real programs hit real problems: missing files, bad input, network hiccups. try/except lets your code handle failure gracefully instead of crashing. else runs when nothing went wrong, and finally always runs — perfect for cleanup.
takeaways: Put risky code in try and the recovery plan in except.
Match specific exceptions (ValueError) before broad ones.
finally always runs — use it for cleanup like closing files.
lessons.code:
try:
    age = int("twenty")
except ValueError:
    print("That is not a number")
    age = 0
finally:
    print("Done, age =", age)

quiz.q: When does the except block run?
options: Only when an error occurs in try
Only when there is no error
quiz.why: except runs only if the try block raises a matching exception.

quiz.q: What does finally guarantee?
options: Its code runs whether or not an error happened
quiz.why: finally executes no matter how the try block exits.

quiz.q: What does this print? try: x = 1/1, except ZeroDivisionError: x = 0, print(x)
quiz.why: No error occurs, so the except block is skipped.

quiz.q: Why put except ValueError before except Exception?
options: Specific handlers must come first or they are never reached
quiz.why: Exception would catch everything first, hiding the specific handler.

quiz.q: What prints? try: raise ValueError("bad"), except ValueError: print("caught")
quiz.why: raise triggers the matching except block.

lessons.title: Lambda, map, filter
lessons.explain: Sometimes a full def is overkill — lambda creates a tiny throwaway function right where you need it. map applies a function to every item, filter keeps only the items that pass a test, and sorted with a key function sorts by anything you can compute. Together they are a compact toolkit for transforming data.
takeaways: lambda n: n * 2 is a tiny function with no name.
map(f, items) transforms; filter(f, items) keeps matches.
sorted(items, key=...) sorts by whatever the key function returns.
lessons.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
doubled = list(map(lambda n: n * 2, nums))
print(doubled)
evens = list(filter(lambda n: n % 2 == 0, nums))
print(evens)

quiz.q: What is a lambda?
quiz.why: lambda defines a small function inline without a name.

quiz.q: What does map do?
options: Applies a function to every item
quiz.why: map runs the given function on each item and yields the results.

quiz.q: What is list(filter(lambda n: n > 2, [1, 2, 3, 4]))?
quiz.why: filter keeps only the items where the test is True.

quiz.q: What is sorted([3, 1, 2], key=lambda x: -x)?
quiz.why: Sorting by -x puts the largest value first.

quiz.q: Can a lambda body have multiple statements?
options: Yes, as many as you like
quiz.why: A lambda body must be a single expression.

challenge.code:
nums = [5, 2, 8]
print(sorted(nums, key=lambda n: -n))
challenge.hint: Sorting by -n puts the biggest number first.

lessons.title: *args & **kwargs
lessons.explain: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple, and **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict. Together they make flexible functions that accept any number of arguments.
takeaways: *args gathers extra positional args into a tuple.
**kwargs gathers extra keyword args into a dict.
Use *args/**kwargs to forward arguments to other functions.

quiz.q: What type does *args collect arguments into?
quiz.why: *args always packs extra positional arguments into a tuple.

quiz.q: In def f(a, *args, **kwargs):, where do extra keyword arguments go?
quiz.why: **kwargs collects any extra keyword arguments into a dictionary.

quiz.q: What does f(*[1, 2]) do when calling f(a, b)?
options: Passes the list as one argument
Unpacks the list into a and b
quiz.why: The * in a call unpacks an iterable into separate positional arguments.

challenge.hint: join() glues the tuple items with the separator string.

lessons.title: Exception Hierarchy & Custom Exceptions
lessons.explain: All exceptions inherit from BaseException, and your own error types just subclass Exception. Raising a custom exception makes your code's failures self-documenting.
takeaways: Every built-in error (ValueError, TypeError...) inherits from Exception.
class MyError(Exception): pass creates your own exception type.
Catch specific exceptions; bare except: hides bugs.

quiz.q: What should a custom exception inherit from?
quiz.why: Subclassing Exception plugs your error into Python's normal exception handling.

quiz.q: Why avoid a bare except: ?
options: It also catches real bugs and things like KeyboardInterrupt
quiz.why: A bare except swallows everything, including bugs you actually want to see.

quiz.q: What is the parent of ValueError?
quiz.why: All normal errors derive from Exception, which derives from BaseException.

challenge.hint: A custom exception IS an Exception, so except Exception catches it.

lessons.title: Raising Exceptions & Assertions
lessons.explain: raise lets you signal errors deliberately, and assert states assumptions that should never be false. Both turn silent wrongness into loud, debuggable failures.
takeaways: raise ValueError('msg') throws an error with your message.
assert x > 0, 'msg' crashes if the condition is False.
Use raise for bad input; assert for impossible internal states.

quiz.q: What happens when assert 2 + 2 == 5 runs?
quiz.why: A failed assert raises AssertionError immediately.

quiz.q: When should you use raise instead of assert?
quiz.why: raise is for expected runtime errors like bad input; asserts can be disabled with -O.

quiz.q: What does raise ValueError('bad') do?
quiz.why: raise stops execution and throws the exception with your message.

challenge.code:
def check(n):
    assert n >= 0, "negative!"
    return n * 2

print(check(5))
challenge.hint: 5 >= 0 is True, so the assert passes quietly.

lessons.title: try/except/else/finally: The Full Picture
lessons.explain: else runs only when no exception occurred, and finally runs no matter what — perfect for cleanup. Using all four blocks makes your error handling precise instead of guessy.
takeaways: else: runs only if the try block succeeded — put success code there.
finally: always runs, even on return or uncaught errors.
Keep try blocks small so you know exactly what might fail.

quiz.q: When does the else block of try/except/else run?
options: Only if no exception was raised
Only if an exception was raised
quiz.why: else means 'the try succeeded, so do the success path here'.

quiz.q: When does finally run?
options: Always, even after return or an error
Only if there is no else
quiz.why: finally is guaranteed cleanup — it runs no matter how the try exits.

quiz.q: Why keep try blocks small?
options: So you know exactly which line might fail
Big try blocks are a syntax error
quiz.why: A tiny try block pinpoints the risky operation instead of hiding bugs elsewhere.

challenge.hint: The exception skips else; finally still adds 1 to -1.

lessons.title: Iterators & the Iterator Protocol
lessons.explain: An iterator is an object with __next__() that hands out one item at a time; iter() gets one from any iterable. for loops are just pretty wrappers around this protocol.
takeaways: iter([1, 2]) returns an iterator; next(it) pulls the next item.
When items run out, next() raises StopIteration.
Custom classes become iterable by defining __iter__ and __next__.
lessons.code:
it = iter(["a", "b"])

print(next(it))
print(next(it))

for x in [10, 20]:
    print(x)

quiz.q: What does next(it) do when the iterator is exhausted?
quiz.why: StopIteration is the signal that there are no more items — for loops catch it silently.

quiz.q: What does iter([1, 2, 3]) return?
quiz.why: iter() builds a fresh iterator object that tracks position separately from the list.

quiz.q: Which two methods make a custom iterator?
quiz.why: __iter__ returns the iterator and __next__ produces each item — that is the protocol.

challenge.code:
it = iter([5, 6])
first = next(it)
rest = list(it)
print(first)
print(rest)
challenge.hint: The first next() consumes 5, so list() only sees what is left.

lessons.title: Generator Expressions & itertools
lessons.explain: Generator expressions (x*2 for x in data) compute values lazily, one at a time — perfect for huge sequences. itertools adds pro tools like count(), cycle(), and chain() for combining iterables.
takeaways: (x*x for x in range(10**9)) uses almost no memory — values are made on demand.
itertools.count(5) is an infinite counter; pair with islice to take a few.
itertools.chain(a, b) loops over a then b as one stream.
lessons.code:
import itertools

gen = (x * x for x in range(5))
print(list(gen))

combo = itertools.chain("ab", [1, 2])
print(list(combo))

quiz.q: How is (x for x in data) different from [x for x in data]?
options: It is lazy — values are produced one at a time
It is faster for small lists
quiz.why: Parentheses make a generator: nothing is computed until you iterate.

quiz.q: What does itertools.chain('ab', [1]) yield?
quiz.why: chain flattens its arguments into one continuous stream of items.

quiz.q: Why use a generator for 10**9 items?
options: It never stores them all in memory
quiz.why: A generator holds only its current state, so memory stays tiny no matter the size.

challenge.code:
import itertools

c = itertools.count(10)
print([next(c) for _ in range(3)])
challenge.hint: count(10) starts at 10 and steps by 1.

lessons.title: Closures & Higher-Order Functions
lessons.explain: A closure is a function that remembers variables from the scope where it was created. Functions that take or return other functions — like decorators do — are called higher-order functions.
takeaways: An inner function keeps access to its enclosing function's variables.
return inner (no parens) hands back the function itself.
Higher-order functions take functions as args or return them.
lessons.code:
def make_adder(n):
    def adder(x):
        return x + n
    return adder

add5 = make_adder(5)
print(add5(10))
print(add5(20))

quiz.q: What does make_adder(5) return?
options: A function that adds 5 to its argument
quiz.why: It returns the inner adder function, which still remembers n=5.

quiz.q: What makes adder a closure?
options: It remembers n from make_adder's scope
quiz.why: A closure captures variables from its enclosing scope even after that scope exits.

quiz.q: What is a higher-order function?
options: One that takes or returns functions
quiz.why: Treating functions as values — passing or returning them — is the definition.

challenge.hint: square remembers exp=2, so it computes 6**2.

lessons.title: Testing Your Algorithms: Writing Good Tests
lessons.explain: An algorithm you cannot test is an algorithm you cannot trust. A good test suite checks the normal case, the edge cases (empty input, single item, duplicates), and the case that used to fail — with assert statements that fail loudly the moment something breaks.
takeaways: Test normal cases, edge cases (empty, single item), and duplicates.
assert condition stops the run with AssertionError when it fails.
Write the test from the expected answer, not from what the code does.
One small test per behaviour beats one giant test that checks everything.

quiz.q: A good test checks...
options: Normal cases, edge cases, and empty input
quiz.why: Bugs hide in edges and empty inputs, not in the obvious normal case.

quiz.q: What does assert do when its condition is False?
quiz.why: A failed assert raises AssertionError immediately, so a broken test cannot pass quietly.

quiz.q: Why test the empty-input case?
options: Edge cases are where bugs hide
quiz.why: Empty input is the most common crash site — loops, indexing, and max() all misbehave there.

challenge.code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

assert add(2, 3) == 5
print("Test passed")
challenge.hint: The assert holds, so the code keeps going to the print.

lessons.title: Generators for Large Data
lessons.explain: A generator function uses yield to hand out one value at a time, so a million-item sequence costs almost no memory. You can sum it, loop over it, or feed it to another function without ever building a list.
takeaways: `yield` turns a function into a generator that produces values lazily.
A generator holds only its current state, not the whole sequence.
Once a generator is exhausted, it yields nothing more — make a new one.

quiz.q: How is a generator different from a list?
options: A generator stores all values at once
A generator makes values one at a time, using little memory
A generator can be indexed like a list
quiz.why: A generator computes each value on demand and never stores the whole sequence.

quiz.q: What happens after you fully consume a generator?
options: It is exhausted and yields nothing more
quiz.why: A generator is single-use; once it is done, iterating again gives nothing.

quiz.q: Which uses the least memory for 10 million numbers?
options: A list built with append in a loop
They all use the same memory
quiz.why: A generator expression like (x for x in range(10**7)) holds only one value at a time.

challenge.code:
g = (x * x for x in range(4))
print(sum(g))
print(sum(g))
challenge.hint: The first sum uses up the generator — what is left for the second?

lessons.title: Error Handling in Real Programs
lessons.explain: Real programs meet bad input all the time: a mistyped number, a missing file, a zero divisor. Wrapping the risky part in try/except and catching only the specific error keeps the program running and the bug visible.
takeaways: Catch the specific error, like `ValueError` — never hide every error with a bare `except:`.
`else` runs only when the try block succeeds; `finally` always runs.
A helper that returns `None` on bad input turns crashes into data you can check.

quiz.q: Why catch ValueError specifically instead of a bare except?
options: So unrelated bugs are not silently hidden
quiz.why: A bare except swallows real bugs too; catching one type leaves the rest visible.

quiz.q: When does the else block of try/except/else run?
options: When no exception happens in the try block
quiz.why: else is the success path — it runs only if the try block finished cleanly.

quiz.q: What does safe_int("oops") return?
quiz.why: int('oops') raises ValueError, which safe_int catches and turns into None.

challenge.hint: 10 / 2 is a float division; the second call hits the except branch.

lessons.title: Logging in Practice
lessons.explain: print() is fine for quick checks, but real programs use the logging module: every message carries a level — DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR — and you can send logs to a file or silence the chatty ones with one setting.
takeaways: Levels go DEBUG < INFO < WARNING < ERROR; only messages at or above the set level show.
`logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)` sets the level in one line.
`stream=sys.stdout` sends logs to standard output so they show up wherever prints do.
Logs can carry timestamps and go to a file — print() cannot do either.
lessons.code:
import logging, sys

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s: %(message)s", stream=sys.stdout)

logging.info("Phonebook loaded")
logging.warning("Bo has no phone number")
logging.error("Could not save contacts")
logging.debug("This stays hidden")

quiz.q: What is the order of logging levels from quietest to loudest?
quiz.why: DEBUG is the most detailed, ERROR the most severe.

quiz.q: Why use logging instead of print() in a real program?
options: Logs carry a level and can go to a file or include timestamps
quiz.why: Levels let you filter noise, and handlers can write logs to a file for later.

quiz.q: With level=logging.WARNING, which message shows?
quiz.why: Only WARNING and above show; DEBUG and INFO are below the threshold.

challenge.code:
import logging, sys

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING, format="%(levelname)s: %(message)s", stream=sys.stdout)
logging.info("started")
logging.warning("low disk")
challenge.hint: INFO sits below the WARNING threshold, so it is filtered out.

lessons.title: Virtual Environments in Practice
lessons.explain: A virtual environment is a private copy of Python for one project, so its packages never clash with another project's. You create it once with python -m venv, activate it, and pip installs everything inside it.
takeaways: `python -m venv .venv` creates a private environment in a .venv folder.
Activate it, then `pip install` puts packages inside the environment only.
`pip freeze > requirements.txt` records exact versions so anyone can rebuild it.
lessons.code:
import os, sys

print(sys.executable)
print(sys.prefix)
print(os.environ.get("VIRTUAL_ENV", "No virtual environment active"))
print(sys.version.split()[0])

quiz.q: What does a virtual environment do for a project?
options: Isolates a project's packages from other projects
quiz.why: Each venv has its own packages, so two projects can use different versions of the same library.

quiz.q: Which command creates a virtual environment named .venv?
quiz.why: python -m venv .venv builds the environment in a .venv folder.

quiz.q: After activating a venv, where does pip install packages?
options: Into the active environment, not system Python
quiz.why: Activation points pip at the venv's own site-packages folder.

challenge.code:
commands = ["python -m venv .venv", "source .venv/bin/activate", "pip install requests"]
print(len(commands))
print(commands[0])
challenge.hint: Count the setup steps, then take the first one.

lessons.title: Type Hints in Practice
lessons.explain: Type hints are notes on your functions — def add(a: int, b: int) -> int — that say what types you expect. Python ignores them at runtime, but they make code self-documenting and let tools like mypy catch mistakes before you run it.
takeaways: `def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:` hints the argument and return types.
Hints do NOT enforce types at runtime — wrong types still run.
Run `mypy` to check hints statically; read `f.__annotations__` to see them.

quiz.q: Do type hints stop you passing the wrong type at runtime?
options: No — they are notes; Python still runs the code
quiz.why: Hints are ignored at runtime; only a static checker like mypy enforces them.

quiz.q: In def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:, what does -> int mean?
options: It converts the result to int
quiz.why: The arrow annotates the return type.

quiz.q: Which tool checks type hints without running your code?
quiz.why: mypy reads your hints and reports type mistakes statically.

challenge.code:
def double(n: int) -> int:
    return n * 2

print(double(21))
print(double("21"))
challenge.hint: Hints are only notes — Python still runs the code, and a string times 2 repeats it.

lessons.title: List Comprehensions & Lambdas
lessons.explain: Comprehensions build lists in one expressive line — [expr for x in items if cond]. They're faster to read and often faster to run than manual loops. Lambdas are tiny anonymous functions, perfect for short transformations you pass to sorted(), map() or filter().
takeaways: [x**2 for x in range(5)] builds a list in a single line.
Add if to filter: [x for x in items if x > 0].
lambda args: expr creates a throwaway one-line function.
lessons.code:
squares = [x**2 for x in range(1, 11)]
print("Squares:", squares)

evens = [x for x in range(20) if x % 2 == 0]
print("Evens:", evens)

nums = [5, 2, 9, 1]
print("Sorted desc:", sorted(nums, key=lambda x: -x))

quiz.q: [x**2 for x in range(3)] equals…
quiz.why: range(3) gives 0, 1, 2 — and their squares are 0, 1, 4.

quiz.q: A lambda is…
quiz.why: lambda creates a small anonymous function, e.g. lambda x: x * 2.

quiz.q: What is "-".join([str(n) for n in range(3)])?
quiz.why: The comprehension makes ['0','1','2'], then join glues them with '-'.

quiz.q: sorted(['bb', 'a', 'ccc'], key=len) gives…
quiz.why: key=len sorts by length: 1, 2, 3.

quiz.q: What is (lambda x: x * 3)(4)?
quiz.why: The lambda is called immediately with 4.

challenge.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
print([n * 2 for n in nums if n % 2 == 0])
challenge.hint: Filter keeps 2 and 4, then doubles each → [4, 8].

lessons.title: Generators & yield
lessons.explain: Generators produce values lazily — one at a time, using almost no memory. yield pauses the function, hands out a value, and resumes where it left off when asked for the next one. Perfect for huge or infinite sequences that would never fit in a list.
takeaways: yield turns a function into a generator that produces values on demand.
Generators are memory-efficient: items are made one at a time.
(expr for x in items) is a generator expression — like a comprehension but lazy.
lessons.code:
def fibonacci(n):
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(n):
        yield a
        a, b = b, a + b

print(list(fibonacci(10)))

# Memory-friendly: squares of 1M numbers, one at a time
gen = (x**2 for x in range(1_000_000))
print("First 3:", [next(gen) for _ in range(3)])

quiz.q: What does yield do?
quiz.why: yield hands out a value and freezes the function's state until the next value is requested.

quiz.q: Why use a generator for a million items?
quiz.why: Items are produced one at a time instead of building a giant list in memory.

quiz.q: What does this print? def g(): yield 1, yield 2, then print(list(g()))
quiz.why: list() pulls both yielded values out of the generator.

quiz.q: What does next() do to a generator?
options: Resumes it until the next yield
quiz.why: Each next() continues execution from after the last yield.

quiz.q: Why does the second list(gen) print []? gen = (x for x in range(3)), print(list(gen)), print(list(gen))
quiz.why: A generator cannot be rewound; once consumed, it stays done.

challenge.code:
def gen():
    yield 1
    yield 2
g = gen()
print(next(g))
challenge.hint: next() resumes the generator up to the first yield → 1.

lessons.title: Decorators
lessons.explain: Decorators wrap functions to add behaviour — timing, logging, caching, access control — without touching the function's own code. The @ syntax applies a decorator cleanly. Under the hood, @timer on f is just f = timer(f).
takeaways: @decorator above def applies wrapper logic around the function.
The wrapper uses *args, **kwargs to accept any arguments.
@wraps(func) preserves the original function's name and docstring.

quiz.q: What does @timer above def slow_add do?
options: Wraps it to add timing behaviour
quiz.why: The decorator replaces slow_add with wrapper, which times the call then returns the result.

quiz.q: Why use @wraps(func) inside a decorator?
quiz.why: Without it, the wrapped function would report the wrapper's name instead of the original.

quiz.q: With the lesson's @shout decorator, greet() returns…
quiz.why: wrapper() returns func().upper().

quiz.q: When is shout(greet) actually applied?
quiz.why: Decoration happens once, at function definition time.

quiz.q: A decorator whose outer function forgets return wrapper causes…
options: TypeError when calling the decorated function
quiz.why: The name gets bound to None instead of a function.

challenge.hint: @shout replaces greet with wrapper, which uppercases the result.

lessons.title: Modules, pip & Virtual Environments
lessons.explain: Modules organise code into importable files. pip installs third-party packages from PyPI. Virtual environments (venv) give each project its own isolated set of packages so versions never clash. This trio is the professional Python workflow — learn it now and every future project gets easier.
takeaways: import brings in stdlib or third-party modules; pip installs them.
python -m venv venv creates an isolated environment per project.
pip freeze > requirements.txt locks exact versions for sharing.
lessons.code:
# mymath.py  →  import mymath
# def square(x): return x * x

# In your terminal:
#   python -m venv venv        # create isolated environment
#   source venv/bin/activate   # activate it
#   pip install requests       # install a package
#   pip freeze > requirements.txt   # lock dependencies

import math, random
print("π ≈", round(math.pi, 4))
print("Lucky number:", random.randint(1, 100))

quiz.q: What does pip install requests do?
quiz.why: pip is Python's package installer; it fetches packages from PyPI.

quiz.q: Why use a virtual environment?
quiz.why: Each project gets its own package versions — no conflicts between projects.

quiz.q: What does this print? import math, print(math.floor(3.9))
quiz.why: floor() rounds down to 3.

quiz.q: What does pip freeze > requirements.txt do?
options: Saves the exact installed package versions
quiz.why: It records precise versions so others can recreate the environment.

quiz.q: After import random, how do you call randint?
quiz.why: Names live under the module namespace.

challenge.prompt: Fill the blank to create a virtual environment named venv:
challenge.code: python -m ___ venv
challenge.hint: The stdlib module for virtual environments is called venv.

lessons.title: Decorators in Practice
lessons.explain: A decorator is a function that wraps another function to add behavior — logging, timing, access checks — without touching its code. The @ syntax is just shorthand for passing your function through the decorator. Once you see the pattern, you will spot decorators everywhere in real Python projects.
takeaways: @decorator above def is shorthand for func = decorator(func).
The wrapper function runs extra code before/after the original.
Decorators keep cross-cutting concerns (timing, logging) out of business logic.

quiz.q: What does @shout above "def greet" do?
options: Passes greet through the shout decorator
quiz.why: @shout is shorthand for greet = shout(greet).

quiz.q: What must a decorator return?
quiz.why: The decorator returns the replacement function that gets called instead.

quiz.q: What does this print? def shout(func): def wrapper(): return func().upper(), return wrapper, then @shout, def greet(): return "hello", print(greet())
quiz.why: wrapper() returns func().upper().

quiz.q: With @a above @b above def f, which decorator applies first?
quiz.why: Decorators apply bottom-up: f = a(b(f)).

quiz.q: Why should the wrapper accept *args, **kwargs?
options: So it works with any arguments
quiz.why: The wrapper must forward whatever arguments the wrapped function takes.

challenge.hint: The wrapper adds one star on each side of the result.

lessons.title: Generators & Iterators
lessons.explain: Generators produce values one at a time, pausing at each yield and resuming on demand. That laziness means you can work with huge or even infinite sequences without building them all in memory. for loops and next() both know how to pull values from a generator.
takeaways: yield pauses a function and emits one value; next() resumes it.
Generators are lazy — values are produced only when asked for.
A generator is single-use: once exhausted, it stays exhausted.

quiz.q: How is yield different from return?
options: It pauses the function and resumes later, producing a sequence
quiz.why: yield suspends the function state; the next call continues after it.

quiz.q: Why are generators memory-friendly?
options: They produce one item at a time instead of building a whole list
quiz.why: Laziness means only one value exists in memory at a time.

quiz.q: What does this print? def c(n): while n > 0: yield n, n -= 1, then print(list(c(3)))
quiz.why: It yields 3, then 2, then 1.

quiz.q: What does for x in countdown(3): do with the generator?
options: Pulls values one by one until exhausted
quiz.why: for keeps calling next() until StopIteration.

quiz.q: Calling next() on an exhausted generator raises…
quiz.why: Exhaustion is signaled with StopIteration.

challenge.code:
def gen():
    yield 1
    yield 2
g = gen()
print(next(g))
print(next(g))
challenge.hint: Each next() call resumes where the generator paused.

lessons.title: Decorators with Arguments & functools.wraps
lessons.explain: A decorator factory is a function that takes arguments and returns the real decorator. Inside it, @functools.wraps(fn) copies the wrapped function's name, docstring, and metadata onto the wrapper so debugging and docs keep working.
takeaways: A decorator with arguments is really a factory: outer call takes args, inner function is the decorator.
Always apply @functools.wraps(fn) to your wrapper to preserve __name__ and __doc__.
The wrapper usually takes (*args, **kwargs) so it works with any signature.

quiz.q: What does @functools.wraps(fn) do inside a decorator?
options: Copies __name__, __doc__ and other metadata from fn onto the wrapper
Prevents the decorator from being applied twice
quiz.why: wraps updates the wrapper's metadata to look like the original function.

quiz.q: In the example, what does repeat(2) return?
options: A decorator: a function that takes fn and returns the wrapper
quiz.why: repeat(2) returns decorator, which is then applied to greet as @repeat(2).

quiz.q: Without functools.wraps, what would greet.__name__ be after decoration?
quiz.why: Without wraps, the name of the replacement function (wrapper) leaks through.

challenge.hint: tag('math') runs first and returns deco; deco then receives add.

lessons.title: Concurrency I: Threading Basics
lessons.explain: Threads let one program juggle several tasks that spend most of their time waiting, like downloads or file reads. You start them with threading.Thread, wait with join(), and protect shared data with a Lock.
takeaways: Threads shine for I/O-bound work, not CPU-bound number crunching (see the GIL lesson).
Always join() every thread you start so the main program waits for them.
Guard shared mutable state with threading.Lock to avoid race conditions.
lessons.code:
import threading

results = []
lock = threading.Lock()

def work(n):
    with lock:
        results.append(n * n)

threads = [threading.Thread(target=work, args=(i,)) for i in range(5)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
print(sorted(results))

quiz.q: Why do we call t.join() on each thread?
options: To wait until the thread finishes before the program continues
To give the thread a higher priority
quiz.why: join() blocks the calling thread until that thread completes.

quiz.q: What is threading.Lock() used for?
options: Stopping two threads from mutating shared data at the same time
quiz.why: Only one thread can hold the lock, so the critical section runs atomically.

quiz.q: Threads in CPython are a poor fit for which workload?
options: CPU-heavy computation, because of the GIL
quiz.why: The GIL stops threads from running Python bytecode in parallel on multiple cores.

challenge.hint: join() guarantees every thread finished appending before the print runs.

lessons.title: Concurrency II: asyncio Basics
lessons.explain: asyncio runs many tasks on a single thread with an event loop. Coroutines declared with async def pause at await, letting other tasks run while they wait — no threads, no GIL fights.
takeaways: Write coroutines with async def and pause them with await.
asyncio.gather() runs coroutines concurrently and returns results in order.
asyncio.run(main()) starts the event loop from normal synchronous code.
lessons.code:
import asyncio

async def fetch(name):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return "data:" + name

async def main():
    out = await asyncio.gather(fetch("a"), fetch("b"), fetch("c"))
    print(out)

asyncio.run(main())

quiz.q: What does await do inside a coroutine?
options: Pauses this coroutine so the event loop can run others until the awaited thing completes
quiz.why: await yields control back to the event loop instead of blocking.

quiz.q: asyncio.gather(a(), b(), c()) returns results in which order?
options: The order the coroutines were passed in
quiz.why: gather preserves argument order regardless of completion order.

quiz.q: Which call runs an async main() from regular code?
options: await main() at module top level
quiz.why: asyncio.run() creates the event loop, runs the coroutine, and closes the loop.

challenge.code:
import asyncio

async def double(x):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return x * 2

async def main():
    print(await asyncio.gather(double(1), double(2), double(3)))

asyncio.run(main())
challenge.hint: gather keeps the order of its arguments in the result list.

lessons.title: The GIL & Multiprocessing
lessons.explain: The Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, so threads can't speed up CPU-bound code. The multiprocessing module sidesteps the GIL with separate processes, each with its own interpreter and memory.
takeaways: The GIL means one thread runs Python bytecode at a time per process.
multiprocessing gives true parallelism for CPU-bound work via separate processes.
Processes don't share memory: data is pickled back and forth, so keep payloads small.

quiz.q: What does the GIL actually prevent?
options: Two threads executing Python bytecode truly in parallel
Two separate processes running at once
Using more than one CPU core for separate programs
quiz.why: The GIL is per-process; separate processes each have their own.

quiz.q: Why guard multiprocessing code with if __name__ == "__main__"?
options: So child processes re-importing the module don't spawn more children
It makes the code run faster
It is required for every Python script
quiz.why: On some platforms children re-import the module, which would re-execute the spawn code.

quiz.q: How do processes exchange data compared to threads?
options: They don't share memory; data is serialized (pickled) between them
They cannot exchange data at all
quiz.why: Each process has isolated memory, so arguments and results are pickled.

challenge.hint: Pool.map applies the function to each item and preserves input order.

lessons.title: Generators: send(), Coroutines & Pipelines
lessons.explain: Calling .send(value) on a generator feeds a value in as the result of the currently-paused yield expression. That turns generators into coroutines you can chain into lazy data-processing pipelines.
takeaways: yield both produces a value outward and receives the next send() value inward.
Prime a coroutine with next(gen) before the first send().
Chain small generators so each stage lazily transforms the stream.
lessons.code:
def averager():
    total = 0.0
    count = 0
    while True:
        x = yield total / count if count else 0.0
        total += x
        count += 1

avg = averager()
next(avg)
avg.send(10)
avg.send(20)
print(avg.send(30))

quiz.q: In 'x = yield 10', what does gen.send(99) do?
options: Resumes the generator with x bound to 99
Restarts the generator from the top
quiz.why: send() resumes at the paused yield and the expression evaluates to the sent value.

quiz.q: Why call next(gen) before the first send()?
options: The generator must run to its first yield before it can receive a value
It is optional style with no effect
quiz.why: A just-created generator hasn't started; only None can be sent before the first yield.

quiz.q: What do generator-based pipelines buy you?
quiz.why: Each stage yields items on demand instead of building giant intermediate lists.

challenge.code:
def doubler():
    total = 0
    while True:
        x = yield total
        total += x * 2

g = doubler()
next(g)
print(g.send(5))
print(g.send(3))
challenge.hint: Trace it: after send(5), total is 0 + 5*2 = 10, which is then yielded.

lessons.title: functools Toolkit: lru_cache, partial, reduce
lessons.explain: functools packs three high-leverage helpers: lru_cache memoizes expensive pure functions, partial freezes some arguments of a function, and reduce folds an iterable into a single value.
takeaways: @lru_cache(maxsize=None) memoizes pure functions: same args, instant answer.
partial(fn, a) returns a new callable with argument a pre-filled.
reduce(fn, iterable, start) folds left; pair it with the operator module for clean code.

quiz.q: What does @lru_cache do?
options: Caches return values so repeated calls with the same arguments are instant
Runs the function on multiple cores
quiz.why: It memoizes: a cache keyed by arguments stores past results.

quiz.q: What does partial(int, base=2) return?
options: A callable like int but with base pre-set to 2
quiz.why: partial freezes arguments, returning a new callable awaiting the rest.

quiz.q: reduce(operator.add, [1, 2, 3], 10) equals?
quiz.why: Start at 10, then 10+1+2+3 = 16.

challenge.code:
from functools import lru_cache

calls = []

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def f(x):
    calls.append(x)
    return x * 10

f(2)
f(2)
f(3)
print(len(calls), f(2))
challenge.hint: The second f(2) hits the cache, so the body runs only twice total.

lessons.title: Type Hints & Static Checking
lessons.explain: Type hints like def f(x: int) -> int document intent and let tools like mypy catch bugs before runtime. Python itself ignores them completely — they're metadata for humans and checkers, not enforcement.
takeaways: Hints are documentation plus tooling; Python never enforces them at runtime.
Use list[int], dict[str, int], and X | None for modern container and optional hints.
Run mypy or pyright in CI to catch type errors before they ship.
lessons.code:
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b

print(add(2, 3))
print(add.__annotations__)

quiz.q: Does Python enforce type hints at runtime?
options: No: they are ignored at runtime; tools like mypy check them statically
quiz.why: Hints live in __annotations__; nothing checks them unless you run a checker.

quiz.q: What does add.__annotations__ hold?
options: The parameter and return annotations as a dict
Nothing: the attribute does not exist
quiz.why: Annotations are stored in a plain dict on the function object.

quiz.q: How do you hint 'a list of ints' on modern Python (3.9+)?
quiz.why: Builtin generics like list[int] work since Python 3.9.

challenge.hint: Hints are not enforced: 'x' + 'y' is perfectly valid string concatenation.

lessons.title: Logging Done Right
lessons.explain: The logging module replaces print-debugging with leveled, configurable output. Get a logger per module with getLogger(__name__), log at the right level, and configure handlers and formatting once at startup.
takeaways: Use logging.getLogger(__name__) per module instead of the root logger directly.
Levels ascend: DEBUG < INFO < WARNING < ERROR < CRITICAL.
Configure once with basicConfig or dictConfig; library code should never print().
lessons.code:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s: %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("app")
log.debug("hidden")
log.info("started")
log.warning("careful")

quiz.q: With level=logging.INFO, which call produces no output?
quiz.why: DEBUG is below the INFO threshold, so it is filtered out.

quiz.q: Why prefer logging over print() for diagnostics?
options: Levels, timestamps, and routing to files or handlers without code changes
quiz.why: Logging separates the decision to record from where the record goes.

quiz.q: What does logging.getLogger('app') return on the second call?
options: The same logger object as the first call
quiz.why: Loggers are cached by name in a registry; same name, same object.

challenge.code:
import logging
log = logging.getLogger("demo")
print(log.name)
print(log.getEffectiveLevel() == logging.WARNING)
challenge.hint: A fresh logger inherits the default WARNING level from the root logger.

lessons.title: Debugging with pdb
lessons.explain: pdb is Python's built-in debugger: calling breakpoint() drops you into an interactive shell at that line. Step with n, continue with c, inspect values with p, and quit with q.
takeaways: breakpoint() starts a pdb session at that line (Python 3.7+).
n runs the next line, c continues, p <expr> prints a value, q quits.
Use pp for pretty-printing and l to see surrounding source.
lessons.code:
def divide(a, b):
    # breakpoint()  <- drop in here: try p a, then n, then c
    return a / b

print(divide(10, 2))

quiz.q: What does breakpoint() do?
options: Opens an interactive pdb session at that line
quiz.why: It invokes the built-in debugger right where it is called.

quiz.q: In pdb, what does the 'n' command do?
options: Executes the current line and moves to the next one
quiz.why: n means next: step over the current line.

quiz.q: How do you inspect a variable's value inside pdb?
quiz.why: p evaluates and prints the expression in the current frame.

challenge.prompt: If you put breakpoint() on the s += x line, pdb would show s as 1, then 3, then 6. What does the program print?
challenge.hint: The debugger only observes; the loop still sums 1 + 2 + 3.

lessons.title: Packaging: Ship Your Own pip Package
lessons.explain: Shipping a package means a pyproject.toml describing your project plus your code in a package directory. pip install -e . installs it editable for development, and python -m build plus twine take it to PyPI.
takeaways: pyproject.toml holds name, version, dependencies, and the build backend.
Keep importable code in a package directory with an __init__.py.
pip install -e . for local development; build with python -m build.
lessons.code:
# myapp/__init__.py
__version__ = "1.0.0"

def hello(name):
    return "Hello, " + name + "!"

print(__version__)
print(hello("pip"))

quiz.q: What does pyproject.toml describe?
options: Project metadata: name, version, dependencies, build system
quiz.why: It is the standard manifest pip and build tools read.

quiz.q: What does pip install -e . do?
options: Installs the local package in editable mode so changes take effect immediately
quiz.why: Editable installs link to your working directory instead of copying.

quiz.q: Where does importable package code live?
options: In a directory with an __init__.py (or a namespace-package directory)
quiz.why: The package directory is what Python puts on the import path.

challenge.code:
__version__ = "2.5.0"
major, minor, patch = __version__.split(".")
print(major, int(minor) + int(patch))
challenge.hint: split('.') gives ['2', '5', '0']; add the last two as integers.

lessons.title: Profiling & Optimization
lessons.explain: Profile before you optimize: cProfile shows where your program really spends time, and timeit gives trustworthy micro-benchmarks. Most real wins come from better algorithms, not micro-tweaks.
takeaways: cProfile plus pstats finds the actual hotspots: measure, don't guess.
timeit.repeat avoids one-off timing noise for fair comparisons.
Optimize algorithms first; readability beats cleverness everywhere else.
lessons.code:
import cProfile, pstats, io

def slow():
    return sum(i * i for i in range(10000))

pr = cProfile.Profile()
pr.enable()
slow()
pr.disable()
out = io.StringIO()
pstats.Stats(pr, stream=out).print_stats(1)
print("profiled ok")

quiz.q: What is cProfile for?
options: Measuring where your program spends its time
quiz.why: It records per-function call counts and cumulative time.

quiz.q: Why use timeit instead of time.time() around code once?
options: It repeats the measurement and reduces timing noise for stable results
It runs the code in parallel
quiz.why: Repetition plus setup control makes micro-benchmarks trustworthy.

quiz.q: What is the first rule of optimization?
options: Measure first: profile before changing anything
quiz.why: Guessing hotspots wastes effort; profilers show the truth.

challenge.code:
import timeit
t1 = timeit.timeit('"-".join(str(n) for n in range(100))', number=100)
t2 = timeit.timeit('"-".join(map(str, range(100)))', number=100)
print(t1 > 0 and t2 > 0)
challenge.hint: Both timings are positive durations, so the comparison is always True.

lessons.title: Pythonic Idioms Masterclass
lessons.explain: Pythonic code leans on the language: comprehensions, zip, enumerate, any/all, unpacking, and context managers. These idioms are shorter, often faster, and instantly readable to experienced Python developers.
takeaways: Prefer comprehensions and any()/all() over manual accumulator loops.
Unpack with a, b = ... and a, *rest = ...; iterate pairs with zip and enumerate.
Idiomatic code is a feature: it signals intent to every Python reader.
lessons.code:
words = ["  Hello ", "WORLD", " python "]
clean = [w.strip().lower() for w in words]
print(clean)
pairs = dict(zip(["a", "b"], [1, 2]))
print(pairs)
print(any(x > 5 for x in [1, 9, 3]))

quiz.q: Which is the most Pythonic way to build a doubled list?
options: map() with a lambda stored in a variable
A while loop with a manual index
quiz.why: The comprehension states the transformation directly and idiomatically.

quiz.q: What does a, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4] bind?
quiz.why: The starred target collects all remaining items into a list.

quiz.q: Why is any(x > 5 for x in xs) better than a manual loop?
options: It short-circuits on the first match and reads as pure intent
quiz.why: any() stops early and the generator expresses the condition directly.

challenge.code:
data = [("a", 1), ("b", 2), ("c", 3)]
letters, nums = zip(*data)
print(letters)
print(sum(nums))
challenge.hint: zip(*data) unzips: first elements together, second elements together.

lessons.title: Decorators: Building a Timer & Cache
lessons.explain: A timer decorator wraps a function, records the start time, calls it, and reports how long it took. Pair that idea with functools.lru_cache and you get the two most common real-world decorators: measure it, then memoize it.
takeaways: A timer decorator uses time.perf_counter() before and after the wrapped call.
Always use @functools.wraps(fn) so the wrapper keeps the original name and docstring.
@lru_cache(maxsize=None) memoizes pure functions: repeated calls with the same arguments return instantly.

quiz.q: Why use time.perf_counter() in a timer instead of time.time()?
options: It is a monotonic high-resolution clock made for measuring durations
quiz.why: perf_counter is designed for benchmarking: it never jumps backwards when the system clock changes.

quiz.q: What does @lru_cache do on the second call fib(10)?
options: Returns the cached result without re-running the body
quiz.why: The cache is keyed by arguments, so a repeat call is a hit, not a recomputation.

quiz.q: Why does the timer decorator apply @functools.wraps(fn) to the wrapper?
options: To hide the wrapper from debuggers
To preserve the original function name and docstring
quiz.why: Without wraps, introspection sees the wrapper, not the real function.

challenge.code:
from functools import lru_cache

calls = []

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def double(x):
    calls.append(x)
    return x * 2

double(3)
double(3)
double(4)
print(len(calls), double(3))
challenge.hint: The second double(3) is a cache hit, so the body runs only for 3 and 4.

lessons.title: Decorators: Retry & Rate Limiting
lessons.explain: A retry decorator re-runs a flaky function a few times before giving up, which is how you survive a brief network hiccup. A rate-limit decorator does the opposite job: it slows calls down so you never exceed an API quota.
takeaways: Retry only transient errors, and give up after a small number of attempts.
Add a short sleep between attempts so a struggling service can recover.
Rate limiting tracks the time of the last call and sleeps until the next one is allowed.

quiz.q: In the example, why does fetch() succeed on the third call?
options: The retry decorator re-runs it until it stops raising ValueError
quiz.why: retry(3) allows three attempts; the first two raise, the third returns 42.

quiz.q: What should a retry decorator do after the final failed attempt?
options: Re-raise the exception so the caller knows it failed
quiz.why: Swallowing the error would hide a real failure; the caller needs to know.

quiz.q: Why put a sleep between retry attempts?
options: To give the failing service a moment to recover
To make the code slower on purpose
quiz.why: Hammering a struggling service instantly usually just fails again; a pause helps.

challenge.hint: retry(2) allows two attempts, then the exception escapes.

lessons.title: Context Managers: @contextmanager
lessons.explain: The @contextmanager decorator from contextlib turns a generator function into a context manager: code before yield is the setup, the yielded value is bound by as, and code after yield is the cleanup, which runs even if the block raises.
takeaways: @contextmanager turns a generator into a with-ready object.
Code before yield sets up; code after yield cleans up, like __exit__.
Wrap the yield in try/finally so cleanup runs even when the block raises.
lessons.code:
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def timer():
    print("start")
    yield "go"
    print("stop")

with timer() as signal:
    print(signal)

quiz.q: In a @contextmanager generator, what does the yield do?
options: It hands the value to the as-target and pauses until the block ends
It returns from the function permanently
quiz.why: The generator pauses at yield; when the with block exits it resumes after yield for cleanup.

quiz.q: Why wrap the yield in try/finally?
options: It is required for every generator
So cleanup runs even if the with block raises an exception
To make the code run faster
quiz.why: An exception in the block is thrown into the generator at the yield; finally guarantees cleanup.

quiz.q: What does @contextmanager save you from writing?
quiz.why: The decorator builds the context manager protocol from a single generator function.

challenge.code:
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def tag():
    print("in")
    yield 5
    print("out")

with tag() as value:
    print(value)
challenge.hint: Setup prints first, then the block body, then the cleanup after yield.

lessons.title: Asyncio: Tasks & Gathering Results
lessons.explain: asyncio.create_task() schedules a coroutine to run in the background while your code carries on, and await asyncio.gather() collects the results of several tasks at once. The results always come back in the order you passed the tasks, not the order they finished.
takeaways: asyncio.create_task(coro) schedules a coroutine to run concurrently.
await asyncio.gather(*tasks) waits for all of them and returns results in argument order.
Cancel a task with task.cancel() when you no longer need its result.
lessons.code:
import asyncio

async def work(name):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return name + " done"

async def main():
    tasks = [asyncio.create_task(work(n)) for n in ("a", "b", "c")]
    print(await asyncio.gather(*tasks))

asyncio.run(main())

quiz.q: What does asyncio.create_task() do?
options: Converts a coroutine into a normal function
Schedules a coroutine to run concurrently on the event loop
Runs the coroutine immediately and blocks
quiz.why: It wraps the coroutine in a Task and schedules it; the loop runs it when it can.

quiz.q: await asyncio.gather(t1, t2) returns results in which order?
options: The order the tasks were passed in
quiz.why: gather preserves argument order in its result list regardless of completion order.

quiz.q: What happens if one task passed to gather raises?
options: gather raises that exception (and by default the other tasks keep running)
It returns None for that task
quiz.why: By default gather propagates the first exception; pass return_exceptions=True to collect errors as results instead.

challenge.code:
import asyncio

async def square(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return n * n

async def main():
    print(await asyncio.gather(square(2), square(3), square(4)))

asyncio.run(main())
challenge.hint: gather returns a list in the order the coroutines were passed.

lessons.title: Asyncio: Async File & Network IO
lessons.explain: Async code shines when waiting on files or the network, but you still need the right tool for each: use asyncio.to_thread for blocking file reads, and an async HTTP client for real requests. Here the network reply is sample data, exactly what an API would hand you, so nothing touches the real network.
takeaways: asyncio.to_thread() runs blocking calls like open() without freezing the event loop.
Never call requests.get inside a coroutine: it blocks the whole loop.
Parse the response with json.loads whether it came from a real API or sample data.
lessons.code:
import asyncio
import json

sample = "{\"name\": \"Ava\", \"score\": 92}"

async def fetch_user():
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return json.loads(sample)

def _read(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        return f.read()

async def main():
    with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
        f.write("hello async")
    user = await fetch_user()
    text = await asyncio.to_thread(_read, "notes.txt")
    print(user["name"], user["score"], text)

asyncio.run(main())

quiz.q: Why use asyncio.to_thread() for reading a file inside a coroutine?
options: Files cannot be opened in async code at all
open() blocks, and to_thread runs it off the event loop so other tasks keep moving
quiz.why: A blocking call inside a coroutine would freeze the whole loop; to_thread moves it to a worker thread.

quiz.q: Why does this lesson parse sample JSON instead of calling a real API?
options: So the code runs offline and deterministically, exactly as a real response would look
json.loads only works on sample data
quiz.why: The sample string is shaped like a real API response, so the parsing code is identical but needs no network.

quiz.q: What would a blocking requests.get() do inside a coroutine?
options: Freeze the entire event loop until the response arrives
quiz.why: The loop is single-threaded: a blocking call stalls every task, not just the current one.

challenge.code:
import asyncio
import json

async def fake_get():
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return json.loads("{\"city\": \"Pune\", \"temp\": 28}")

async def main():
    data = await fake_get()
    print(data["city"], data["temp"])

asyncio.run(main())
challenge.hint: fake_get returns the parsed sample dict; the prints just read its keys.

lessons.title: Threading: Locks & Race Conditions
lessons.explain: A race condition happens when two threads read and write the same value at the same time, so updates get lost. A threading.Lock makes the read-modify-write step atomic: only the thread holding the lock can be inside that block, so no update is ever lost.
takeaways: A race condition is lost or corrupted updates from unsynchronised shared access.
Wrap the critical section in with lock: so only one thread runs it at a time.
Keep the locked section as small as possible so threads are not waiting on each other.

quiz.q: Why does the example print exactly 4000 every time?
options: The lock makes each increment atomic, so no update is lost
Python integers are thread-safe by themselves
quiz.why: With the lock, the read-add-write of counter[0] cannot be interleaved with another thread.

quiz.q: What is a race condition?
options: Two threads interleaving access to shared data so the result depends on timing
Two threads racing to finish first
A thread that runs too fast
quiz.why: The outcome depends on the unpredictable interleaving of the threads.

quiz.q: What happens if a thread forgets to release a lock it acquired?
options: Other threads block forever waiting for it (deadlock)
The lock releases itself after one second
quiz.why: A lock stays held until released, so a missing release stalls every waiter; use with lock: to avoid it.

challenge.code:
import threading

total = [0]
lock = threading.Lock()

def add(n):
    with lock:
        total[0] += n

ts = [threading.Thread(target=add, args=(5,)) for _ in range(3)]
for t in ts:
    t.start()
for t in ts:
    t.join()
print(total[0])
challenge.hint: Three threads each add 5 under the lock, and join waits for all of them.

lessons.title: Multiprocessing: Pools & Queues
lessons.explain: A multiprocessing Pool spreads CPU-heavy work across processes, each with its own interpreter, so the GIL cannot slow you down. A Queue is how those separate processes send results back: a worker puts values in, and the main process gets them out.
takeaways: Pool.map(fn, items) runs fn on each item across worker processes and keeps input order.
Processes do not share memory: results travel back through a Queue (pickled).
Always close or context-manage the pool and join() processes so nothing is left running.

quiz.q: Why use a Pool instead of threads for squaring a million numbers?
options: Processes sidestep the GIL, so CPU work truly runs in parallel
quiz.why: Each process has its own interpreter and GIL, so CPU-bound work scales across cores.

quiz.q: How does a child process send a result back to the parent?
options: By returning from the target function
Through a Queue (or the Pool return value); processes do not share memory
By writing to a shared global variable
quiz.why: Memory is isolated per process, so results must be pickled through a Queue or collected by the Pool.

quiz.q: Why guard the pool code with if __name__ == __main__?
options: It is required for every Python file
So child processes re-importing the module do not spawn more children
quiz.why: On spawn-based platforms children re-import the module, which would re-run the pool creation.

challenge.hint: Pool.map applies the function to each item and preserves input order.

lessons.title: Testing: pytest Fundamentals
lessons.explain: pytest finds functions whose names start with test_ and runs them, reporting any failed assert as a failure. You do not need a test class or special methods: a plain function and a plain assert are a complete test, and you can run the same functions directly to see them pass.
takeaways: Name test functions test_something so pytest discovers them.
Use plain assert statements: pytest shows exactly which values differed.
Run tests with pytest in the terminal; each function here also runs directly as a demo.

quiz.q: How does pytest discover a test function?
options: It is defined in a class
quiz.why: pytest collects functions and files matching the test_ naming pattern.

quiz.q: What does pytest do when an assert fails inside a test?
options: Reports that test as FAILED and shows the values that differed
quiz.why: A failed assert is the signal: pytest catches it and reports the mismatch.

quiz.q: Why write several small tests instead of one big test?
options: A failure points at exactly the broken behaviour instead of a vague block
quiz.why: One behaviour per test makes failures precise and the suite easier to read.

challenge.hint: Both asserts hold, so both test functions return without raising.

lessons.title: Testing: Fixtures & Parametrize
lessons.explain: A fixture is a reusable setup helper that builds the fresh data each test needs, so tests never share state. Parametrize runs the same test once per input case, so one test function covers a whole table of examples instead of copy-pasting the same check.
takeaways: A fixture builds fresh data per test; tests should never share mutable setup.
In pytest, @pytest.fixture marks the setup function and tests receive it by name.
@pytest.mark.parametrize runs one test over a list of (input, expected) cases.

quiz.q: What problem does a fixture solve?
options: It replaces the code under test
Every test gets fresh setup data instead of sharing mutable state
quiz.why: Shared setup leaks state between tests; a fixture rebuilds it per test.

quiz.q: What does @pytest.mark.parametrize do?
options: Runs the same test once for each case in a list
quiz.why: Each parameter set becomes its own test run with its own pass or fail.

quiz.q: In the example, how many times does test_average run?
options: 0 times: it is only a helper
quiz.why: The loop feeds the three cases in one by one, mirroring parametrize.

challenge.hint: All three cases hold, and len(cases) is 3.

lessons.title: Testing: Mocking External Services
lessons.explain: A mock is a fake object that stands in for a real service during a test, returning canned answers you control. You test your own logic, like how you handle a returned user, without ever calling the real API, database, or payment service.
takeaways: Mock the boundary (API, database, network) and test your own logic against canned answers.
unittest.mock.Mock lets you set return_value and check call_count afterwards.
Pass the dependency in (dependency injection) so tests can swap in a mock.
lessons.code:
from unittest.mock import Mock

def greet(client, user_id):
    user = client.get_user(user_id)
    return "hi " + user["name"]

fake = Mock()
fake.get_user.return_value = {"name": "Ava"}
print(greet(fake, 7))
print(fake.get_user.call_count)

quiz.q: Why mock an external service in a test?
options: So the test is fast, offline, and deterministic instead of depending on a live service
Mocks make the real service faster
quiz.why: A live service can be slow, flaky, or charge money; a mock returns exactly what you set.

quiz.q: What does fake.get_user.return_value = {...} do?
options: Makes every call to fake.get_user() return that dict
quiz.why: return_value is the canned answer the mock hands back on every call.

quiz.q: How can you check the mock was actually used?
quiz.why: Mocks record every call, so you can assert your code called the service exactly as expected.

challenge.code:
from unittest.mock import Mock

def score_of(client, user_id):
    return client.get_user(user_id)["score"]

fake = Mock()
fake.get_user.return_value = {"score": 92}
print(score_of(fake, 1))
print(fake.get_user.call_count)
challenge.hint: The mock returns the canned dict, and it was called exactly once.

lessons.title: Testing: Coverage & CI Basics
lessons.explain: Coverage measures which lines of your code your tests actually execute, so you can see the untested corners. Continuous integration runs the whole suite on every push, so a broken change is caught by the server instead of by your users.
takeaways: Coverage reports the percentage of lines your tests execute; aim high on core logic, not 100% everywhere.
Run pytest --cov=. to generate a coverage report.
In CI, the pipeline installs dependencies, runs pytest, and fails the build on any failing test.

quiz.q: What does code coverage measure?
options: Which lines of code your tests actually execute
quiz.why: Coverage instruments the code and reports the executed lines versus the missed ones.

quiz.q: What does a CI pipeline do on every push?
options: Installs dependencies and runs the test suite, failing the build on any failure
quiz.why: CI gives every change the same automated check before a human reviews it.

quiz.q: Why is 100% coverage a weak goal on its own?
options: It measures lines executed, not whether the asserts actually check the right behaviour
quiz.why: A test can execute a line without asserting anything useful about it.

challenge.code:
def double(x):
    return x * 2

tests = [lambda: double(2), lambda: double(3)]
passed = 0
for t in tests:
    assert t() == 4 or t() == 6
    passed += 1
print(passed, "/", len(tests), "tests passed")
challenge.hint: double(2) is 4, so the first assert passes at once; double(3) is 6, so the second assert passes via the or's second check (t() == 6).

lessons.title: Packaging: Wheels, pyproject & Publishing
lessons.explain: Packaging turns your code into something others can install with pip. A pyproject.toml file declares the name, version and dependencies, and building it produces a wheel — a ready-to-install .whl file you can upload to PyPI.
takeaways: `pyproject.toml` is the modern home of package metadata: name, version, and dependencies.
A wheel filename looks like `mytool-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl`: name, version, Python tag, platform tag.
`python -m build` builds the wheel; `twine upload` publishes it to PyPI.
lessons.code:
project = {"name": "skillzify-tools", "version": "0.1.0", "requires-python": ">=3.10"}
print(project["name"], project["version"])
wheel = project["name"].replace("-", "_") + "-" + project["version"] + "-py3-none-any.whl"
print("wheel name:", wheel)

quiz.q: What is pyproject.toml for?
options: Declaring a package name, version, and dependencies for building
quiz.why: Build tools read pyproject.toml to know what they are packaging.

quiz.q: What is a wheel (.whl) file?
options: A compressed backup of your project
A pre-built package archive that pip can install directly
quiz.why: Wheels are the installable format pip downloads from PyPI.

quiz.q: In the wheel name mytool-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl, what is 0.1.0?
quiz.why: Wheel names follow name-version-python-abi-platform, so 0.1.0 is the version.

challenge.code:
project = {"name": "quiz-app", "version": "2.3.1"}
print(project["name"] + " " + project["version"])
challenge.hint: The plus joins the two strings with the space in between.

lessons.title: Profiling: Finding Bottlenecks
lessons.explain: Profiling means measuring where your program actually spends its time instead of guessing. A one-line timing test can prove that a set lookup beats a list scan by a hundred times — and that is the kind of fact you optimize on.
takeaways: `timeit.timeit(code, setup=..., number=1000)` times a snippet fairly by repeating it.
Set and dict lookups are near-instant even at 10,000 items; list scans grow with size.
Profile first, optimize second: measure the real hotspot before rewriting code.
lessons.code:
import timeit

list_time = timeit.timeit("9999 in xs", setup="xs = list(range(10000))", number=1000)
set_time = timeit.timeit("9999 in xs", setup="xs = set(range(10000))", number=1000)
print("set faster:", set_time < list_time)
print(list_time > 0 and set_time > 0)

quiz.q: Why use timeit instead of timing code once with time.time()?
options: Repeating the measurement averages out noise and gives a stable result
timeit runs the code in parallel
quiz.why: One run is noisy; hundreds of repeats reveal the real difference.

quiz.q: Why is 9999 in a set of 10,000 items so much faster than in a list?
options: Sets store items in sorted order
Set lookup uses a hash and is roughly constant time
quiz.why: Hashing jumps straight to the item instead of scanning from the start.

quiz.q: What is the first step when code feels slow?
options: Measure with a profiler or timeit to find the real hotspot
Rewrite the whole program in another language
quiz.why: Guessing wastes effort; measurement shows where the time actually goes.

challenge.code:
import timeit
t = timeit.timeit("[x * x for x in range(100)]", number=100)
print(t > 0)
challenge.hint: A timing is always a positive number of seconds.

lessons.title: Caching Strategies: lru_cache & Redis Intro
lessons.explain: Caching means remembering an answer instead of recomputing it. functools.lru_cache remembers function results in memory, while Redis is a separate in-memory server that many processes — or many machines — can share, with keys that expire automatically.
takeaways: `@lru_cache(maxsize=128)` memoizes a function: repeated calls with the same arguments return instantly.
`fn.cache_info()` shows hits, misses, and size so you can prove the cache is working.
Redis is a shared in-memory key-value store with expiry (TTL); use it when the cache must outlive one process.
lessons.code:
from functools import lru_cache

calls = []

@lru_cache(maxsize=128)
def square(n):
    calls.append(n)
    return n * n

print(square(5), square(5), square(6))
print("computed:", len(calls))
print(square.cache_info().hits)

quiz.q: What does @lru_cache do to a function?
options: Deletes the function after one call
Saves results to a database file
Remembers past results so repeated calls with the same arguments skip the work
Makes the function run in parallel
quiz.why: The cache stores argument-to-result pairs and replays them on a hit.

quiz.q: In the example, why is len(calls) 2 after three calls?
options: The second square(5) was a cache hit, so the function body ran only twice
quiz.why: square(5) computed once, then hit the cache; square(6) computed once.

quiz.q: When would you pick Redis over lru_cache?
options: When you only cache one value
When you want the slowest possible cache
When the cache must be shared across processes or machines and survive restarts
When the function has no arguments
quiz.why: lru_cache lives inside one process; Redis is a shared server with expiry.

challenge.hint: The second call with 3 is a hit, not a recomputation.

lessons.title: Code Quality: Linting with Ruff & Black
lessons.explain: Linting catches bugs before they run: Ruff flags unused imports, undefined names, and style slips in milliseconds, while Black reformats your code to one consistent style. Together they make every file look like it was written by the same careful developer.
takeaways: Ruff is a linter: it flags unused imports, undefined names, and style problems without running your code.
Black is a formatter: it rewrites spacing and line breaks to one standard style.
Run both in CI so messy code never merges; `py_compile` is a quick syntax sanity check.
lessons.code:
import py_compile, os

open("lint_demo.py", "w").write("x = 1\nprint(x + 1)\n")
py_compile.compile("lint_demo.py", doraise=True)
print("compiles ok:", os.path.exists("lint_demo.py"))
print("ruff would flag: unused import")
print("black would format: x=1  ->  x = 1")

quiz.q: What does a linter like Ruff do?
options: Flags likely bugs and style problems without running the code
quiz.why: Linting is static analysis: it reads the code and reports problems.

quiz.q: What is Black for?
options: Reformatting code to one consistent style
quiz.why: Black only changes formatting, never behaviour.

quiz.q: Why run Ruff and Black in CI (continuous integration)?
options: CI replaces the need to write tests
So style and lint problems are caught on every push before they merge
So code is hidden from reviewers
quiz.why: Automated checks enforce quality on every change, not just when someone remembers.

challenge.code:
import py_compile
open("ok.py", "w").write("a = 2\nprint(a)\n")
py_compile.compile("ok.py", doraise=True)
print("ok")
challenge.hint: doraise only raises on a syntax error, and this file is valid.

lessons.title: CSV in Depth: Real-World Data Cleaning
lessons.explain: Real CSV files are messy: extra spaces, missing values, and blank rows. A good cleaning pass strips whitespace, skips bad rows, and converts text to the right types before you trust the data.
takeaways: `csv.DictReader` reads each row as a dict keyed by the header names.
Use `.strip()` on every field — messy files hide spaces around values.
Missing numbers become `None`, not zero, so you never invent data.
lessons.code:
import csv

rows = [["name", "age", "city"], [" Ava ", "29", " Pune "], ["Bo", "", "Mumbai"], ["", "41", "Delhi"]]
with open("people.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    csv.writer(f).writerows(rows)

clean = []
with open("people.csv", newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        name = row["name"].strip()
        if not name:
            continue
        age = int(row["age"]) if row["age"].strip() else None
        clean.append((name, age, row["city"].strip()))

print(clean)
print(len(clean))

quiz.q: What does csv.DictReader give you for each row?
options: It reads only the first row
It reads each row as a dict keyed by the header names
quiz.why: DictReader uses the header row as keys, so you can write row['name'].

quiz.q: Why should you strip() fields from a real CSV file?
options: To remove surrounding spaces from messy data
quiz.why: Real files often have spaces like ' Ava ' that would break comparisons and lookups.

quiz.q: How should you handle a missing age in a row you keep?
options: Treat it as missing and keep the row if the name is valid
quiz.why: A missing age is None, not zero — the row is still useful without inventing a value.

challenge.code:
import csv, io

data = "name,score\nAl,90\nBo,80\n"
rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(data)))
print(type(rows[1]["score"]).__name__)
challenge.hint: DictReader never converts types — every value arrives as text.

lessons.title: JSON APIs: Fetching Real Data
lessons.explain: Most web APIs hand you JSON text, and json.loads() turns it into Python dicts and lists you can work with. You fetch the text with a library like requests in real code; here you parse a sample of exactly what an API would return.
takeaways: `json.loads(text)` turns a JSON string into Python dicts and lists.
Navigate the result with keys and indexes, just like any nested dict.
Use `.get("key")` when a field might be missing, to avoid KeyError.
lessons.code:
import json

# In a real program this string is what the API returns;
# you would fetch it with requests, then parse it the same way.
sample = "{\"city\": \"Pune\", \"temp_c\": 28, \"condition\": \"Sunny\", \"forecast\": [{\"day\": \"Mon\", \"temp_c\": 29}, {\"day\": \"Tue\", \"temp_c\": 27}]}"
data = json.loads(sample)

print(data["city"], data["temp_c"])
print(data["forecast"][0]["day"], data["forecast"][0]["temp_c"])
print(len(data["forecast"]))

quiz.q: What does json.loads() do?
options: Turns a JSON string into Python dicts and lists
Turns Python data into JSON text
quiz.why: loads parses JSON text into the matching Python objects.

quiz.q: What does data["forecast"][0]["day"] get from the weather data?
quiz.why: [0] takes the first forecast entry, and ['day'] takes its day name.

quiz.q: Why use .get("key") instead of ["key"] on API data?
options: It returns None instead of raising KeyError if the key is missing
quiz.why: APIs sometimes omit fields, and .get() handles a missing key gracefully.

challenge.code:
import json

data = json.loads("{\"users\": [{\"name\": \"Ava\"}, {\"name\": \"Bo\"}]}")
print(len(data["users"]))
print(data["users"][1]["name"])
challenge.hint: Index 1 is the second user — count the list first, then pick the name.

lessons.title: Data Science: NumPy Arrays
lessons.explain: A NumPy array is a grid of numbers of one type, stored compactly so whole-array maths runs in fast compiled code. You build one with np.array(), check its shape, and operations like a * 2 apply to every element at once with no Python loop.
takeaways: np.array([1, 2, 3]) creates a 1-D array; .shape tells you its dimensions.
Array operations are element-wise: a * 2 doubles every element at once.
np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3) builds a 2-row, 3-column grid.
lessons.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a * 2)
print(b.shape)
print(np.zeros(3))

quiz.q: What does np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3) create?
quiz.why: arange(6) makes 0-5 and reshape(2, 3) lays them out in 2 rows of 3.

quiz.q: What does a * 2 do when a is a NumPy array?
options: Repeats the array twice like a list
Doubles every element, returning a new array
quiz.why: NumPy operators are vectorised: they apply element-wise across the whole array.

quiz.q: What does b.shape return for a 2-row, 3-column array?
quiz.why: shape is a tuple of sizes, rows first, then columns.

challenge.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.shape)
print(a + 10)
challenge.hint: The array is 2 by 2, and adding 10 shifts every element.

lessons.title: Data Science: NumPy Indexing & Broadcasting
lessons.explain: NumPy slicing picks rows and columns with m[:, 1], and boolean masks pick elements that pass a test, like a[a > 2]. Broadcasting stretches a smaller array to match a bigger one, so a column of shape (2, 1) can add to every column of a (2, 3) grid without a loop.
takeaways: m[:, 1] selects a whole column; m[0, :] selects a whole row.
Boolean masks like a[a > 2] return only the matching elements.
Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right: (2, 1) plus (1, 3) gives (2, 3).
lessons.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
m = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(m[:, 1])
print(a[a > 2])
col = np.array([[10], [20]])
print(col + np.array([1, 2, 3]))

quiz.q: What does m[:, 1] return for a 2-row, 3-column array m?
options: The whole second column as a 1-D array
quiz.why: The colon means all rows; 1 picks column index 1.

quiz.q: What does a[a > 2] return when a is [1, 2, 3, 4]?
quiz.why: The boolean mask selects only the elements where the condition is True.

quiz.q: Broadcasting a (2, 1) array with a (1, 3) array gives what shape?
quiz.why: Dimensions of size 1 stretch to match, so rows and columns combine into (2, 3).

challenge.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([5, 10, 15])
print(a[1:])
print(a + 100)
challenge.hint: a[1:] drops the first element; adding 100 shifts every remaining one.

lessons.title: Data Science: pandas Series & DataFrames
lessons.explain: pandas is the go-to library for tabular data in Python. A Series is one labelled column of data, and a DataFrame is a table made of Series sharing one index — think of it as a spreadsheet you can program.
takeaways: A `Series` is a one-dimensional labelled array; a `DataFrame` is a two-dimensional table of rows and columns.
Pick a column with `df['score']` and a single value with `df['score'].mean()` or label-based indexing.
Check a table's size at a glance with `df.shape`, which returns `(rows, columns)`.
lessons.code:
import pandas as pd
scores = pd.Series([88, 92, 79], index=["Ava", "Bo", "Al"])
print(scores["Bo"])
df = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Ava", "Bo"], "score": [88, 92]})
print(df["score"].mean())
print(df.shape)

quiz.q: What is a pandas DataFrame?
options: A Python list that only holds numbers
A two-dimensional table of rows and columns with labels
quiz.why: A DataFrame is a labelled table: rows and columns you can select, filter and summarise.

quiz.q: Which of these creates a Series with the labels a and b?
quiz.why: The index= argument sets the labels; there is no labels= argument.

quiz.q: What does df.shape return for a table with 2 rows and 3 columns?
quiz.why: shape is always (rows, columns), so 2 rows and 3 columns gives (2, 3).

challenge.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([10, 20, 30], index=["a", "b", "c"])
print(s["b"] + s["c"])
challenge.hint: Labels pick values: s['b'] is 20 and s['c'] is 30.

lessons.title: Data Science: Cleaning Data with pandas
lessons.explain: Real data is messy: missing values, duplicates, wrong types. pandas gives you a small toolkit for this — isna() to find the gaps, dropna() or fillna() to deal with them, and drop_duplicates() to remove repeats — before you trust any analysis.
takeaways: Find missing values with `df['col'].isna().sum()`; pandas represents them as `NaN`.
Use `dropna()` to remove rows with gaps, or `fillna(value)` to replace the gaps.
Remove repeated rows with `drop_duplicates()` and check the shape before and after.
lessons.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Ava", "Bo", "Al"], "score": [88, None, 79]})
print(df["score"].isna().sum())
clean = df.dropna()
print(clean.shape)
print(clean["score"].mean())

quiz.q: What does df.dropna() do?
options: Removes rows that contain missing values
quiz.why: dropna drops any row (by default) that contains a NaN.

quiz.q: What does fillna(0) do?
quiz.why: fillna replaces each NaN with the value you pass, here 0.
